#5735. Energy drinks linked to 11 times more reports of cardiac arrest

Energy drinks and stimulant supplements are raising new concerns about heart health after researchers discovered a striking pattern in reports of serious cardiovascular emergencies. Products containing caffeine and other stimulants appeared far more frequently in reports of cardiac arrest, heart attacks, and other heart problems than products without these ingredients.

The findings were particularly concerning among younger adults. People ages 18 to 34 accounted for a substantial share of the reported heart problems involving caffeinated products, according to independent, preliminary research presented at the American Heart Association's Scientific Sessions 2026.

Researchers emphasized that the findings do not establish that energy drinks or stimulant supplements caused these medical emergencies. However, the unusually high frequency of certain cardiovascular events in FDA safety reports suggests that these widely available products deserve closer examination.

Growing Concerns About Energy Drinks and Heart Health

The energy drink industry has expanded rapidly, with sales more than doubling over the past decade and exceeding $20 billion in 2024. Despite their popularity, scientists still have limited information about the cardiovascular effects of energy drinks and supplements containing stimulants.

Existing evidence suggests that consuming large amounts of caffeine can harm the cardiovascular system. Medical professionals have also documented cases of arrhythmias (irregular heart rhythms) and sudden cardiac death following the consumption of these products. Some of these incidents involved young adults who had no previously identified risk factors for heart disease.

A 2026 American Heart Association Scientific Statement on caffeine and cardiovascular disease indicates that most adults can generally consume up to 400 mg of caffeine daily without significant safety concerns (the equivalent of up to 5, 8-ounce cups of regular black caffeinated coffee).

However, caffeine concentrations can differ dramatically between products. Certain energy drinks provide up to three times as much caffeine per fluid ounce as brewed coffee, while some pre-workout supplements contain more than 12 times the concentration found in coffee.

Another concern involves how these products are regulated. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) classifies energy drinks and stimulant supplements as foods or dietary supplements rather than medications. As a result, they are not subject to the same safety testing requirements that medications must meet before entering the market.

"These products are marketed as everyday pick-me-ups and sold next to soda and bottled water, so most people assume they carry no real risk," said study author Sai Samayamanthula, a fourth-year medical student at the University of Virginia School of Medicine in Charlottesville, Virginia. "For many healthy people, if these products are consumed occasionally, the risk is probably small. However, individuals who consume energy drinks or other stimulant-containing supplements regularly can quickly exceed the recommended daily limit for caffeine, so it's important for people to know that there may be a risk of cardiovascular harm with these products."

FDA Reports Reveal Striking Differences in Cardiac Events

To investigate possible cardiovascular safety concerns, researchers examined a federal database containing reports of suspected adverse reactions to foods and dietary supplements. They compared products containing caffeine and other stimulants with products that did not contain these ingredients.

The comparison group included commonly consumed products such as soft drinks, smoothies, vitamins, protein bars, and meal replacement shakes. Researchers examined reports involving people ages 13 and older submitted between 2017 and 2025.

Several differences stood out in the analysis:

These differences describe how frequently certain medical problems appeared within the FDA reports. They do not mean that people consuming energy drinks face an 11 times greater actual risk of cardiac arrest or a 4.5 times greater risk of having a heart attack.

"Our findings support the case for more systematic safety monitoring of caffeine- and stimulant-containing products. In addition, healthcare professionals should remember to ask their younger patients who have palpitations, chest pain, or fainting spells if they recently or regularly consume these products," Samayamanthula said.

Why Young Adults May Be Particularly Vulnerable

One of the most notable findings was the large proportion of cardiovascular reports involving younger adults. Researchers have not yet determined why the connection between stimulant products and reported heart problems appeared so frequently in this age group.

Several explanations are possible. Younger consumers may use energy drinks and stimulant supplements more often, increasing the likelihood that these products appear in reports of medical emergencies.

How the products are consumed could also influence the pattern. Potential contributing factors include the circumstances surrounding their use (for example, consuming them before intense exercise or mixing them with alcohol or drugs). Some individuals may also have previously undiagnosed heart conditions that could make them more susceptible to cardiovascular complications.

These possibilities remain uncertain, and additional research will be needed to determine which factors, if any, help explain the unusually high reporting frequency among younger adults.

Do Energy Drinks Actually Cause Heart Attacks?

Although the results raise important questions about products containing concentrated caffeine and other stimulants, experts caution against interpreting the findings as proof of a direct cause.

"This study raises concerns that products with very high amounts of caffeine may be harmful to the cardiovascular system," said Gregory M. Marcus, M.D., M.A.S., FAHA, chair of the 2026 American Heart Association scientific statement on caffeine and cardiovascular disease. "Although there are biological reasons why that connection could be possible, the study does not prove that caffeine products cause these events, because other factors may have influenced the results found in this analysis. More research is needed to understand whether these stimulant products are truly responsible for the reported heart-related events."

Marcus did not participate in the research. He is a professor of medicine at the University of California, San Francisco School of Medicine and serves as associate chief of the Cardiology for Research program at the University of California, San Francisco Health.

Because the analysis relied on reports submitted voluntarily to the FDA, it cannot establish whether the products themselves were responsible for the cardiovascular events. Other health conditions, behaviors, or circumstances may have played a role.

How Researchers Analyzed the FDA Safety Reports

The research team reviewed 28,345 reports of possible adverse events submitted to an FDA safety database from 2017 through 2025.

Of these, 854 reports involved energy drinks or dietary supplements containing caffeine or other stimulants. The remaining 27,491 reports concerned products without caffeine or stimulant ingredients and served as the comparison group.

Researchers classified products according to the ingredients they contained. The stimulant category included caffeine, methylxanthines (theobromine, guarana, yerba mate, green tea/coffee extracts) and sympathomimetics (synephrine, yohimbine, ephedra, DMAA, higenamine).

Rather than evaluating individual brands, the researchers grouped products by their ingredients. Consequently, the findings apply to broad categories of caffeinated and stimulant products and do not identify any particular brand as more dangerous than another.

The researchers also highlighted important limitations in the available data. Reports were voluntarily submitted by members of the public, consumers, healthcare professionals, and manufacturers, meaning that the database does not provide a complete record of everyone who experienced a possible adverse reaction.

Just as importantly, the researchers could not determine how many people consumed these products without developing cardiovascular problems. They also could not establish how many people experienced heart problems but never submitted a report.

Without those figures, the analysis cannot calculate the actual likelihood of a heart attack, cardiac arrest, or another cardiovascular event among consumers of energy drinks and stimulant supplements.

Nevertheless, the findings reveal a potentially important safety signal. Researchers say more systematic monitoring and further studies are needed to determine whether these products contribute directly to serious heart problems, particularly among younger adults who frequently consume them.

#5733. HLTH 2026: Viz.ai’s chief clinical officer on takeaways, goals of AI collab with National Rural Health Association

HLTH 2026: Viz.ai’s chief clinical officer on takeaways, goals of AI collab with National Rural Health Association" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

It’s been almost seven months since artificial intelligence disease detection and care coordination platform Viz.ai entered into a partnership with the National Rural Health Association (NRHA).

The partnership aims to help rural healthcare leaders better understand and implement AI tools across systems. That's been a personal and professional passion of Viz.ai Chief Clinical Officer Andrew Ibrahim, M.D., who discussed with Fierce Healthcare at HLTH his key takeaways from the collaboration thus far and forward-looking goals as it approaches its one-year mark.

Ibrahim said that the two organizations have done three educational events for rural health systems since the partnership kicked off in April. These series aim to show rural health administrators the specifics of AI—and whether they should adopt it, he said.

He noted there’s “sometimes a very big mismatch” when smaller rural health systems onboard multiple vendors.

“We've learned [that] many rural hospitals don't have the IT expertise and infrastructure to adopt some of these tools, and so it's actually been a force function to strengthen their hub spoke relationships,” Ibrahim said.

Strengthening these relationships, according to Ibrahim, has been key.

“It's actually been beautiful to see the hub-spoke relationship strengthened with the AI tool as the conduit,” Ibrahim said. “And it gives them a reason to interact more, and a way for the rural hospitals to strengthen their capabilities.”

He continued, “there's an authenticity about the moment where it's like ‘Yeah, we do need to help each other out.’ We're all kind of figuring it out as we go.”

In addition to the educational series, Ibrahim said frameworks are in development to aid rural health systems in navigating, implementing and deploying AI—which will be built into a toolkit.

One of Ibrahim’s personal goals for the one-year mark of the partnership is to ensure any rural health administrator can understand what an AI tool is when pitched.

“I think that would be a huge milestone,” he said. “Getting to 100% of hospitals at year one would be ideal—probably unrealistic, but that's probably the ultimate goal.”

And when it comes to metrics for measuring the collaboration, Ibrahim said he's looking for numbers that show participants are “keeping more care local” and retaining their workforces.

“It would be great to be able to connect the dots [and understand whether] adoption of an AI tool give[s] rural clinicians confidence, enthusiasm, willingness to stay in their community as opposed to dropping the services and moving back,” he said.

Another initiative from Viz that has “disproportionate benefit in rural communities,” according to Ibrahim, is its new partnership with Wolters Kluwer Health to integrate the Viz.ai One platform into UpToDate Expert AI.

“I'm pretty excited about being able to bring their level of clinical decision support into our rural hospitals,” he said.

#5732. National Academies report calls for faster decisions on publication retractions and corrections

We ranked the 25 most valuable publicly traded Chinese drugmakers

West Coast Biotech & Life Sciences Reporter

Jonathan Wosen is STAT’s West Coast biotech & life sciences reporter. You can reach Jonathan on Signal at jwosen.27.

A new report commissioned by the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine urged the scientific community to respond more aggressively to claims of errors or manipulated data in published research, saying that papers containing findings that can no longer be trusted should be more swiftly corrected or retracted.

The report encouraged journals to complete editorial review of potentially problematic studies within 12 weeks, or within six months in more complex cases. The authors also stressed that study authors need to hold onto original data, adding that being unable to produce these records when concerns about a finding’s authenticity are raised could lead to a retraction. And the expert panel wrote that it is no longer “prudent” for researchers to argue against retraction of their work by asserting that flawed findings in one part of a study don’t impact the paper’s overall conclusions. That’s because issues with any part of a study can cast doubt on other findings.

The authors called on universities and other research institutions to respond more quickly and completely to research integrity inquiries, in part by making findings from internal inquiries available to journals, funding organizations, and the broader public. And the National Academies report suggested that funding organizations tie grant awards to researchers and institutions agreeing to abide by strict standards for the conduct of research and addressing errors.

“While the committee’s recommendations might appear aspirational, we are certain that the funding agencies, the public officials who legislate financial and regulatory support for science, researchers, and, most importantly, the public must be assured that the record of scientific knowledge is intact and reliable,” wrote University of California, Berkeley, cell biologist Randy Schekman, chair of the committee that produced the report.

An advanced copy of the report was sent to media outlets and embargoed until 11 a.m. EST on Thursday. But Jennifer Walsh, a National Academies spokesperson, told STAT in an email that “the report is being paused pending further review of some of the citations.” She did not provide a new release time and, as of Thursday evening, the report has not been published on the nonprofit’s website. Reporting by Science alleges that 10 of the report’s references contain apparently fabricated first names for co-authors, suggesting that a large language model may have written the references. The National Academies delayed publication after Science flagged the apparent issues.

The 157-page National Academies report comes at a time when concerns about the reliability of the scientific record have drawn increasing public attention, contributing to distrust in scientific institutions. High-profile investigations at leading research centers such as Stanford University and Dana-Farber Cancer Institute have in recent years shined an uncomfortable spotlight on how studies published in top journals can contain doctored data. Meanwhile, the number of scientific articles published each year has risen from 1.3 million in 1995 to 6.7 million in 2025, increasing the number of studies that potentially require corrective action.

Retractions have become more common in recent years, with the report noting that more than 5,000 studies were retracted worldwide in 2025. But the report alleges that this rate is lower than expected given current estimates of the proportion of problematic articles, with fewer than 0.22% of studies from any given year retracted. Data from Retraction Watch indicate that, on average, retractions happen nearly 2.4 years after a study is published.

Correcting the record more often and more quickly, the authors wrote, won’t just require clearer policies from funding organizations, journals, and universities. It will take a cultural shift in science toward viewing correction and retraction as essential tools in maintaining the reliability of the record, not as a professional failure. They encouraged stakeholders to think of the consequences of not taking corrective action on studies, from policymaking and public health decisions made based on faulty data to researchers wasting time and taxpayer dollars when they attempt to follow up on a flawed finding.

“Serious consequences for the scientific enterprise and for society in general result either from failing to correct the scientific record or from failing to do so in a timely way,” the panel wrote. “These consequences make changing the process essential.”

While many corrections and retractions result from honest errors, the Trump administration has cited cases of alleged research misconduct as justification for its focus on “gold standard” science. In the new report, experts noted that these incidents can weaken public trust in science.

“It is critical that the scientific ecosystem continues to prioritize maintaining the integrity of the scientific record so that it remains trusted and trustworthy,” the authors wrote. “Even if these cases are rare, just one such incident erodes the public’s trust.”

That recognition spurred the National Academies, a 163-year-old nonprofit created by Congress to advise the nation on issues of science and technology, to assemble a team of university, journal, and academic leaders to explore what should be done. They included Holden Thorp, editor-in-chief of the Science family of journals; Schekman, a Nobel Prize-winning researcher and former editor-in-chief of the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences; and Mark Barnes, a lawyer with the firm Ropes & Gray and former associate provost for research at Harvard University. The group was tasked with identifying current practices and suggesting new standards for stakeholders.

The authors lay out what they frame as an “ideal timeline” for addressing concerns with published studies. That includes four weeks for an editor to determine whether a concern is potentially credible, meaning that it is specific, makes sense, and merits a closer look. The committee then allots another four weeks for contacting authors and determining whether their response adequately resolves a concern before initiating a full review. They note that an initial notice, such as an editorial expression of concern, should be added to a study within 12 weeks.

It’s a well-intentioned timeline, said Lisa Rasmussen, a bioethicist at the University of North Carolina at Charlotte. But Rasmussen, who is also editor-in-chief of the journal Accountability in Research, said that editors like herself are already stretched thin with work that is often poorly compensated. She noted that, in the past five years, the number of studies submitted to her own journal has increased almost tenfold. Rasmussen and a co-editor-in-chief often message each other with drowning emojis to sum up how they are doing.

“I think under the best of circumstances, it’s very reasonable. That’s certainly the kind of time frame that I try to abide by,” she said. “I think it’s just going to be increasingly difficult for people to handle the volume of concerns [and] queries that they’re receiving in the time frame.”

Rasmussen noted that much of the rise in submissions took place after large language models powered by artificial intelligence, such as ChatGPT, became readily available. The report touches on the impact of AI on research integrity, noting that these tools have simultaneously allowed researchers to manipulate or fake data while giving journals and universities new tools to spot suspect results. But to Rasmussen, the report’s discussion on AI was surprisingly brief given the technology’s disruptive potential.

“AI is being used to review. AI is being used to critique. AI is being used to fabricate data. So it’s like jet fuel for all of the stuff they talk about in the report,” she said. “But it’s almost as though the report was written pre-ChatGPT.”

West Coast Biotech & Life Sciences Reporter

Jonathan Wosen is STAT’s West Coast biotech & life sciences reporter. You can reach Jonathan on Signal at jwosen.27.

#5731. Department of Labor moves to end expedited green cards for nurses, physical therapists

Department of Labor moves to end expedited green cards for nurses, physical therapists" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

The U.S. Department of Labor proposed new policy this week that would end fast-track green cards for healthcare professionals like nurses and physical therapists—the latest in a string of policies from the Trump administration raising the bar for foreign-born workers and students across healthcare and other industries.

Currently, nurses, physical therapists and other workers “with exceptional ability in the sciences or arts” are granted an exemption from an administrative test in the permanent labor certification program (PERM), a months-long administrative process in which an employer must prove there are no able, willing, qualified and available U.S. workers for a permanent job ahead of sponsoring a foreign worker.

The exemption, referred to Schedule A, is given to occupations where the DOL recognizes a nationwide shortage of U.S. workers. Nurses and physical therapists have been listed under Schedule A for more than 30 years.

The Department of Labor, in its newly proposed rule, said it wants to eliminate Schedule A as it cannot “demonstrate that the occupations currently listed in Schedule A are still shortage occupations.”

It cited in the proposed rule a late 2023 request for information published under the Biden administration seeking input on potentially expanding Schedule A. Despite more than 2,000 responses, DOL now says it didn’t receive the information it would need to establish a methodology for regularly reviewing and updating Schedule A occupations, and questioned whether it has the statutory authority to make such occupational exemptions in the first place.

“The elimination of Schedule A would enable the Department to better ensure that U.S. workers have an opportunity to apply for available job opportunities, and adhere to the statutory requirements to protect U.S. workers assigned to it, as intended by Congress under the [Immigration and Nationality Act].”

The proposed rule, which is open to public comment for 60 days, also includes requirements for employers to advertise their open jobs more broadly and for a longer period of time to demonstrate a good-faith effort to recruit American workers before turning to a green card sponsorship. These and other proposed changes would be the first “comprehensive” reforms to the PERM program in almost two decades, the Department of Labor said.

If finalized as-is, employers who want to sponsor professional nurses, physical therapists and other affected roles “would be required to go through the lengthier and costlier PERM labor market testing process, adding time, cost and administrative work to a pathway that hospitals, nursing homes and rehabilitation providers have historically relied on to fill persistent shortages,” Caroline Tang, an Austin shareholder at labor and employment law firm Ogletree Deakins, told Fierce Healthcare.

Industry associations as well as other sections of the government have widely projected shortages in the healthcare workforce, including nurses, for the coming years. The Heart Resources and Services Association’s National Center for Health Workforce Analysis, for instance, projects (PDF) national shortages of registered nurses through at least 2038, with a projected 8% shortage in 2028 that is more severe in non-metro areas.

The proposed policy change is among several brought by the Trump administration in line with an order from the White House to prioritize domestic hiring—though many have been stymied in the courts.

Among the most prominent is a $100,000 supplemental fee the Department of Homeland Security attached to H-1B petitions that was vacated by two separate judged, and in August was succeeded by the somewhat altered proposal of an additional H-1B petition fee of $103,265. Another policy from the same department tightening how long nonimmigrant students may remain in the country (referred to as “duration of status”) was temporary blocked hours before implementation in September and fully vacated on Monday (PDF), though the former decision is already being appealed.

The Department of Labor has also proposed increasing the prevailing wage floors for several green cards that legal experts expect will be challenged by employers that would shoulder the resulting financial burden.

#5730. The Efficacy of Broad Match + Audiences Strategy in Real Estate

When considering digital marketing strategies, the realm of real estate is no different from any other industry. The key objective remains the same - reaching the target audience with an impactful, compelling message that can inspire action. An increasingly popular approach adopted by real estate agents is the broad match + audiences strategy. This approach leverages the power of Google AdWords' broad match feature and combines it with audience targeting to attain superior marketing results.

The real estate sector thrives on the availability of a vast array of properties, each with a unique combination of attributes that appeal to different prospective buyers. Recognizing this immense diversity and matching it with the correct buyer is a daunting challenge that real estate agents constantly grapple with. This is where the broad match + audiences strategy steps in, optimizing the process by expanding reach while ensuring relevance.

The broad match feature in Google AdWords is a type of keyword match that allows your ads to show whenever someone searches for that keyword or a related phrase. It can include searches that are misspellings, synonyms, related searches, and other relevant variations.

With the broad match feature, you're casting a wide net over an extensive range of search queries. It brings with it the advantage of gaining visibility across a wider spectrum of potential buyers who might not use the exact keywords that you've selected for your campaign.

In the real estate industry, property attributes can be incredibly diverse, ranging from "3-bedroom apartments in New York City" to "colonial-style houses with large gardens in Austin". By leveraging the broad match feature, agents can reach potential clients who use various search terms that directly or indirectly relate to their listing.

Audience targeting is a method used in digital marketing to segment audiences based on specific criteria like demographics, interests, buying behavior, etc. Google AdWords allows you to target your ads to specific audiences, ensuring they are seen by those who are most likely to be interested in your offerings.

In the context of real estate, audience targeting can be a game-changer. For instance, if an agent specializes in selling luxury homes, they can target audiences with high-income levels and a demonstrated interest in luxury living. Alternatively, if an agent focuses on properties suitable for first-time buyers, they can target younger audiences who have recently started searching for homes.

The marriage of broad match keywords with audience targeting may seem counter-intuitive at first, considering one aims at breadth and the other at specificity. However, the combination forms a robust strategy that takes the best of both worlds - wide reach and precise targeting.

The broad match feature ensures a wide reach, allowing real estate agents to surface their listings to a large number of prospective clients. But, broad match alone can lead to high impression counts with low conversion rates as the ads may be presented to irrelevant audiences. This is where audience targeting steps in to bring precision.

When used in conjunction, the broad match feature ensures that your ads reach a wide array of searchers, while audience targeting ensures these ads are shown to a specific subset of this wide audience who are most likely to be interested in your property listings.

This synergistic approach allows real estate agents to achieve two key objectives:

In the dynamic and competitive world of real estate, digital marketing strategies need to be both comprehensive and precise. The broad match + audiences strategy does precisely that - it maximizes the reach of property listings while maintaining relevance to the audience. As such, it is not surprising that this strategy is being widely adopted by savvy real estate agents seeking to gain a competitive edge in the digital realm. The power of a wide-reaching yet finely tuned marketing strategy should not be underestimated in a market as diverse and competitive as real estate.

#5729. Walking and weight training may not be enough to keep your bones strong

The type of exercise you do may be more important for your bones than how long you spend doing it. Researchers at Semmelweis University have found that intense physical activity involving sudden bursts of movement, quick changes in direction, and sharp turns appears especially effective at stimulating new bone formation.

The findings, published in Sports Medicine - Open, suggest that certain fast-paced sports may provide greater benefits for bone metabolism than walking or conventional strength training. The research could help scientists develop more effective exercise recommendations for preserving bone health and reducing the risk of osteoporosis.

Why Exercise Intensity Matters for Bone Health

To investigate how different forms of exercise affect bones, the Semmelweis University team reviewed 24 clinical studies involving 1,238 healthy adults.

Instead of relying on bone mineral density measurements, which can take considerable time to reveal changes, the researchers examined blood markers associated with the production of new bone tissue. These biological indicators can reveal how bones respond to exercise within a matter of weeks, allowing scientists to detect changes much sooner.

"What makes our study unique is that we examined not only the type of exercise - whether endurance, resistance, or combined training - but also exercise intensity, frequency, and duration. Our goal was to determine which forms of exercise stimulate bone metabolism most effectively and which appear to be less beneficial from this perspective," said Dr. Péter Ferdinandy, Vice-Rector for Science and Innovations at Semmelweis University and senior author of the study.

Football and Handball Show Surprising Bone Benefits

The strongest responses were associated with vigorous sports that repeatedly require players to accelerate, change direction, turn, and make powerful movements.

Recreational football and handball stood out in particular. These activities were linked to increases of up to 45-46 percent in blood markers associated with bone formation, suggesting that they may provide a particularly strong stimulus for the body's bone-building processes.

More conventional activities generally produced smaller responses. Walking, step aerobics, and standard resistance workouts performed in the gym were less effective at stimulating the measured indicators of bone formation.

The findings were especially unexpected for resistance training, which is commonly recommended as a way to support skeletal health.

"The most surprising finding was that resistance training did not produce a significant effect on markers of bone metabolism, even though several professional guidelines recommend this type of exercise for maintaining bone health. Likewise, low- or moderate-intensity endurance exercise, such as walking or jogging, showed no meaningful long-term effect," explained Viktória Barna, PhD student at Semmelweis University and first author of the study.

Why Walking and Weight Training Still Matter

The results do not suggest that walking, jogging, or other less demanding activities should be abandoned. These forms of exercise continue to offer important health benefits, even if they do not stimulate the measured bone-building processes as strongly as more intense sports.

Rather, the research indicates that maintaining healthy bones may require greater mechanical stimulation than many everyday activities provide. Movements that place more substantial forces on the skeleton appear to produce a stronger response in the biological processes involved in forming new bone.

However, the researchers stress that people should not suddenly begin strenuous exercise without preparing appropriately.

This is especially important for individuals with cardiovascular, musculoskeletal, or metabolic conditions, as well as those who already have osteoporosis. Anyone in these groups who is considering a new activity or a more physically demanding exercise routine should first speak with their treating physician, general practitioner, or a sports medicine specialist. Medical guidance can help determine whether the activity and its intensity are suitable for their health and physical capabilities.

Could High-Intensity Exercise Help Prevent Osteoporosis?

The findings offer a new perspective on how exercise could be used to maintain bone health as people age. While the analysis focused on markers of bone metabolism rather than direct changes in bone density, the results suggest that vigorous activity may encourage early biological changes that support bone formation.

"According to the World Health Organization, regular physical activity offers numerous health benefits. However, our findings suggest that low-intensity exercise alone is not sufficient to stimulate bone metabolism. High-intensity exercise may trigger early beneficial changes in bone formation, potentially helping to slow bone loss and support healthy aging," summarized Dr. Nóra Sydó, clinical specialist and co-author of the study.

The researchers believe that understanding which movements most effectively stimulate bone formation could lead to better exercise programs designed to preserve skeletal strength and help prevent osteoporosis.

For now, the findings highlight an important distinction: staying physically active is beneficial for overall health, but keeping bones healthy over the long term may depend not only on how much people move, but also on how powerfully and dynamically they move.

Materials provided by Semmelweis University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#5727. UnitedHealthcare's new care model leans on community pharmacies

UnitedHealthcare's new care model leans on community pharmacies" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

UnitedHealthcare is teaming up with CPSEN for a new program that will lean on community pharmacists to reach Medicaid patients.

The insurance giant said Wednesday that its through the UHC Pharmacy Care Hub model, pharmacists will work alongside the payer's care managers and providers to help close gaps in care and support management for chronic conditions and other needs.

Participating pharmacies will offer a range of services, including telehealth, medication management, point-of-care testing and personalized supports. The program is built on a hub-and-spoke model, where pharmacists can then help lead the patient to the right site of care or through any follow-up if needed.

These interactions can also help track patterns in emergency care use, and help patients find a more appropriate setting if their needs aren't emergent.

The program is currently available to UnitedHealthcare Medicaid members in seven states: Florida, Kansas, Michigan, Missouri, North Carolina, Tennessee and Virginia. UHC expects to add additional states throughout the year.

Part of the goal, the company said, is to tap into the trust that local pharmacists have in the communities they serve.

“Community pharmacies are trusted, local access points for care,” said Arethusa Kirk, M.D., chief medical officer for UnitedHealthcare Community & State, in the announcement. “This new model expands the services independent pharmacists can help deliver, making it easier for people—especially those facing barriers to care—to get timely support closer to home.”

UHC said that most (89%) of Americans live within five miles of a pharmacy, making these locations an easier option to access for many. This is especially true for individuals who may struggle to find an appointment with a doctor or find transportation to a visit.

For example, a participating pharmacist in North Carolina, Madeline Clark, said in the announcement that a patient came into the pharmacy for a urine test, as she had a potential urinary tract infection. The pharmacy conducted the test and sent the results virtually to a provider through UnitedHealthcare's Doctor Chat tool.

A prescription was then filled for the patient in the same visit, and she was out the door within about 30 minutes.

Clark said the patient was thankful not just for the ease of that trip to the pharmacy but for avoiding a visit to the ER as well.

"Not only was this a lower cost of care in the healthcare system space, but it also was just incredibly helpful for the patient," she said.

Sarah covers how industries like food and tobacco affect Americans’ bodies and minds. Her interests include ultra-processed foods; smoke-free tobacco; and wellness trends like perimenopause products and peptides. Confidential tips can be sent on Signal at sarahlizchar.47.

Peptides are poised to go mainstream with this week’s launches from telehealth companies Hims & Hers and Noom, both of which announced they will be offering prescriptions for eligible patients.

Synthetic peptides are a broad category of short-chain amino acids. Initially popular among bodybuilders, certain drugs in the class have gained traction among a broad swath of people looking to optimize their health — whether to build muscle, feel more energetic, increase libido, or recover from injuries. But many compounded peptides that are marketed to consumers are experimental. They have not been approved by the Food and Drug Administration, nor are there randomized controlled trials showing their safety and efficacy in humans. The Department of Health and Human Services, however, has foregrounded the drugs under health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., an avowed peptide enthusiast.

While peptide prescriptions were already offered by smaller telehealth companies, Hims (with a market cap of more than $3.5 billion) and Noom (a private company valued at $3.7 billion) are two of the industry’s dominant players, making the announcements a pivotal moment for peptides in the United States.

#5725. Superhuman unveils personal AI assistant and expands Go across entire suite

Superhuman Inc., formerly known as Grammarly, today announced the expansion of Go, its proactive artificial intelligence assistant and multi-agent platform, along with updated features across its entire suite.

Among the updates, the company added a new personalized AI assistant in Go that users can name, give work to and ask to watch projects and to-do lists in the background. The new assistant will work across connected tools, suggest next steps, draft content in the user’s voice, and manage a team of other AI agents, with the user always in the loop.

Superhuman also brought agents into Docs and Mail and updated Fathom, the company’s note-taking app, to act as a collaborative, bot-free app that connects natively to every application across the Superhuman suite and captures video, screen sharing, and audio.

“Superhuman is solving for the last mile of AI: the gap between deployment and adoption,” said Chief Executive Shishir Mehrotra. “The best AI shows up for your whole team, not just the power users who go looking for it. It’s embedded in the tools you already use, it works ahead of you, and it collaborates alongside you.”

Superhuman Go is growing with a personal agent that works ahead of a user on their behalf, with their approval. The company said the new Go assistant acts like an extra set of eyes and ears, watching out for users throughout their day, finding tasks they need to do, and keeping up with their “need to know.” It tries to stay ahead of their task list, offers to complete things it can, picks up slack, summarizes meeting notes, and answers important emails or preps for important meetings.

It also writes like the user and gets better over time with direction. It learns from past responses to draft content that sounds like them, refines writing before they hit send, and keeps learning their style to improve over time.

Superhuman said that it added more than 20 new partner agents, which can help pull in expert knowledge and capabilities from enterprise services. For example, a user can connect to Legora AB’s agent for legal intelligence, Databricks Inc.’s Live Metrics agent for metrics and relevant numbers, Amplitude Inc.’s Product check agent to verify product usage claims, and Blackboard Inc.’s Assignment Coach agent to help students improve coursework.

With the rise of personal AI agents such as OpenClaw and Meta Platform Inc.’s Muse, the open-source community, startups and enterprises have begun offering personalized agents that autonomously assist users with day-to-day tasks and work. Anthropic PBC also recently launched Claude Duet, a similar proactive AI agent for professionals and small businesses in private preview, that completes tasks when asked and keeps working in the background.

Superhuman Go agents are now native in Docs, the company’s AI-native collaborative workspace that combines documents, spreadsheets and automated workflows. Users can share a doc with any agent, just mentioning it with @ to hand off work, and it will show up as another collaborator.

Users can add agents with triggers for when to run, and they will interact with the document whether it’s open or not, updating it whenever something changes. This will allow agents to collaborate by adding to the document and changing it by checking email, watching connected apps or checking connected tables, so that the information in the doc stays fresh.

Similarly, agents connect to Mail and every other tool. This means that when drafting an email, agents can suggest content as users type. Superhuman Mail can use agents to pull in information from Slack, meeting notes or internal documents. The company said auto drafts already saves users an average of nine minutes per draft. For a user who replies to four emails a day, that can save about three hours a week.

In addition to these changes, Superhuman said the Go platform software development kit is generally available to partners and customers with new agent-building capabilities. Partners can now easily build and connect their own agents that show up anywhere within Go. The company plans to add more specialized partner agents.

#5724. Colorectal cancer is rising again after 20 years, and scientists don't know why

Colorectal cancer rates are climbing again in the United States after more than two decades of decline, and the troubling increase is affecting far more than younger adults. New research published in NEJM Evidence reveals that the disease is becoming more common across nearly every age group under 70, raising concerns about a growing public health challenge.

Colorectal cancer is already the second leading cause of cancer deaths in the United States and the leading cause among adults younger than 50. Although rising cases in younger people have attracted widespread attention, the latest findings show that the problem extends into older generations. Researchers warn that a continued increase could place additional pressure on the healthcare system as more patients require cancer treatment and long-term care after diagnosis.

Colorectal Cancer Rates Reverse Decades of Decline

To investigate the changing pattern, Caitlin Murphy, PhD, MPH, Professor of Pediatrics and Public Health Sciences at the University of Chicago, and her colleagues examined the latest colorectal cancer incidence data from the National Cancer Institute. Their analysis tracked changes in diagnoses from 2000 through 2023.

The results revealed a significant reversal. In 2000, the age-adjusted colorectal cancer incidence rate was 55.2 cases per 100,000 people. By 2022, that figure had dropped to 36.7. However, the rate increased to 38.3 in 2023, marking the first overall rise after more than two decades of falling rates.

"This is the first time that we have seen an increase in the overall rate since in more than 20 years," Murphy said. She emphasized that the long-standing downward trend had been a major feature of colorectal cancer statistics for decades. The new analysis indicates that rates are now increasing in every age group through ages 65 to 69.

Murphy, an epidemiologist who specializes in colorectal cancer patterns, had anticipated that the increase initially observed in younger adults would eventually become apparent among older people. She attributes this expected progression to a phenomenon called the "birth cohort effect."

This effect describes how people born during the same general period can share risk patterns that become more apparent as they grow older. In this case, individuals born in the 1960s and subsequent decades appear to face an elevated risk of colorectal cancer as they enter middle age and later life.

"I think of a birth cohort effect as the interaction of age and time," Murphy explained. "As people born around the same time move through time and age together, we're going to see more colorectal cancers being diagnosed."

A Sharp Increase Among Adults Ages 45 to 49

One of the most striking findings involved people between 45 and 49 years old. From 2019 through 2023, colorectal cancer incidence in this group increased by 12.76% annually, the largest rise recorded among the age groups examined.

Researchers believe much of this particular increase can be explained by changes in cancer screening recommendations. National guidelines lowered the recommended starting age for routine colorectal cancer screening from 50 to 45, allowing more people to be tested and more previously undetected cancers to be identified.

"That means that screening is doing as we intend it to do -- it's catching cancer earlier," Murphy said.

But increased screening cannot account for the broader pattern. Colorectal cancer rates are also rising among adults ages 65 to 69, while the decline has stalled among those ages 70 to 74. Both populations have historically experienced substantial benefits from screening, and approximately 80% of people in these age groups are current with recommended testing.

These findings are particularly concerning because they suggest that additional, unidentified risk factors could be counteracting some of the progress achieved through decades of cancer screening.

The research team also investigated whether disruptions during the COVID-19 pandemic might have distorted the results. Cancer screenings and diagnoses were affected during the pandemic, potentially changing when cases were detected. However, the upward trend remained even after the researchers removed data from 2020 and 2021. Screening activity had also largely recovered to its earlier levels by January 2021, making pandemic-related disruptions an unlikely explanation for the increase recorded in 2023.

"These results motivate us to understand reasons for this rise, so risk factors can be identified and possibly reduced," said Sonia Kupfer, MD, director of the Gastrointestinal Cancer Risk and Prevention Clinic at UChicago Medicine.

Why Colorectal Cancer Is Rising Across Generations

The growing number of colorectal cancer diagnoses among younger Americans has become a major health concern. American Cancer Society data show that incidence among adults ages 20 to 49 increased by approximately 3% per year between 2013 and 2022.

This increase in colorectal cancer among people younger than 50, often referred to as early-onset colorectal cancer, has drawn considerable public and scientific attention. The latest study suggests that understanding why younger adults are developing the disease more frequently could also help explain what is happening in older populations.

"There are many unique challenges when you're diagnosed with cancer at a young age, so it's important that we shine a spotlight on that problem," Murphy said. "But in terms of understanding the root cause, I think our study shows that we can consider that whatever might be causing colorectal cancer in younger people is now also causing it to increase in older people as well."

The underlying causes remain uncertain, but researchers are investigating whether exposure to chemicals in the environment could play a role.

Murphy and her colleagues are working with Xin Hu, PhD, a toxicologist at Emory University, to examine this possibility. Their approach involves analyzing small blood samples for evidence of thousands of environmental chemical exposures simultaneously. By identifying which substances are associated with potential risks, the team hopes to narrow the list of chemicals that deserve more detailed investigation.

The researchers then plan to collaborate with Kupfer to explore how these chemicals affect colon tissue. To do so, they will use organoids, laboratory-grown models that reproduce important features of the colon. These miniature tissue systems allow scientists to study biological responses in a controlled environment and could help uncover how certain exposures contribute to colorectal cancer.

Why Colorectal Cancer Screening Remains Critical

With cancer rates increasing across a broad range of ages, the researchers emphasize the need to keep tracking national cancer statistics as new registry information becomes available each year.

Murphy cautions that the consequences could become substantial if the current pattern continues. As large numbers of Americans born in more recent decades grow older, rising incidence rates could translate into many additional cancer diagnoses. That would increase demand for medical treatment and services supporting people who survive colorectal cancer.

While scientists work to understand the factors behind the increase, screening remains one of the most effective ways to find colorectal cancer early and reduce the risk of dying from the disease.

Current national recommendations advise adults at average risk to begin regular colorectal cancer screening at age 45 and continue through age 75. For people younger than 45 or older than 75, screening decisions should be tailored to individual circumstances, including family medical history, symptoms, and other health conditions.

Colonoscopy continues to be considered the gold standard for colorectal cancer screening, but patients also have additional testing options. These include newer blood-based screening tests and stool tests that can be completed at home.

"There are several ways to do screening that should be discussed with a clinician, so people know what the different screening tests are intended for and how often these need to be repeated," Kupfer added.

She also stressed that people younger than 45 should not ignore possible warning signs simply because they have not reached the age recommended for routine screening. Those without known genetic or family history risk factors should still seek medical attention if they notice blood in their stool, persistent changes in bowel habits, or unexplained weight loss.

The research, titled "Colorectal cancer among U.S. adults, 2000-2023," received financial support from the National Institutes of Health and the Eli and Edythe Broad Center of Regenerative Medicine and Stem Cell Research Ablon Scholars Program.

Along with Murphy, the study's authors include Folasade P. May of the University of California Los Angeles, Xin Hu of Emory University in Atlanta, and Samir Gupta of the University of California San Diego.

The University of Chicago's medical and biological sciences programs are also continuing to expand their work in cancer research and patient care. In April 2027, UChicago Medicine is scheduled to open the AbbVie Foundation Cancer Pavilion, which will be Chicago's first freestanding cancer pavilion. The facility is intended to bring together advanced diagnostic services, new cancer treatments, research that translates laboratory discoveries into clinical care, and comprehensive support for patients and the surrounding community.

Aetna is rolling out a new program that aims to provide key end-to-end care for pregnant women, new mothers and infants.

The offering, called Aetna For You and Baby, will be available to all expectant mothers enrolled in an Aetna plan. Through the program, moms will be connected to a prenatal visit in their first trimester and a postpartum visit within 12 weeks of the baby's birth.

Women in the program will also be screened for depression both during and after pregnancy to identify any risks.

In addition to supporting the mother both during pregnancy and postpartum, the program aims to give babies a healthy start by providing at least six well visits through their first 15 months, which offer critical tests and screenings, checkups and vaccinations.

The news of the launch was provided first to Fierce Healthcare.

Katerina Guerraz, Aetna's chief operating officer, told Fierce that maternal care often focuses mostly, if not completely, on labor and delivery, though prenatal and postpartum visits play a critical role in driving positive health outcomes.

In its announcement, Aetna notes that data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention show that about 90% of pregnancy-related deaths could have been prevented, with a lack of access to prenatal care and more complete support making for a key barrier.

"This is a national access issue, a quality issue, and it's an affordability problem," she said.

In addition, it's not uncommon for programs that aim to drive better maternal outcomes to lack services for the babies, who in the first year of life undergo a wide array of critical developmental milestones, Guerraz said.

Aetna, as the third-largest insurer in the U.S., sees about 200,000 deliveries a year among its members. That means the success of this program could have a significant impact in a short amount of time, supporting at least 1 million babies over the next five years, she said.

Aetna for You and Baby also builds on a broader push within the company to build a more personalized and simple experience for members. For instance, the company established a program that embeds Aetna nurses in the hospital to support discharge planning and transitions for members, and Guerraz said that holds potential in the maternal care space.

For example, if a baby needs to stay in the neonatal intensive care unit after birth, having an Aetna nurse in the NICU providing additional support to the clinical team and the member would pay dividends, she said.

Aetna is also plugged into Health 100, a sister subsidiary of its parent company, CVS Health, that offers an AI-powered tool to help patients identify healthcare costs and navigate their benefits, even if they're not members of Aetna or Caremark or CVS Pharmacy customers.

Guerraz said the program is designed to offer something that patients can carry with them if their coverage changes.

She added that the team intends to continue iterating on the program and identifying other barriers to care for moms and their babies.

"This is something that we know is going to have a massive impact," she said.

#5720. Healthcare purchasers must weigh hospital quality alongside their prices, Leapfrog says

Healthcare purchasers must weigh hospital quality alongside their prices, Leapfrog says" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Patient safety watchdog The Leapfrog Group released its latest collection of hospital safety grades hand-in-hand with calls for policymakers and stakeholders to consider, or directly tie patient safety reporting to price transparency.

The twice-yearly release brought top marks for 900 out of a total 2,366 graded hospitals, and the lowest “F” score for just three. There were 774 hospitals that earned a “B” grade, 655 a “C” grade, and 35 a “D” grade.

No grades were assigned to another 447 hospitals, a decision the group made after a judge’s ruling in a lawsuit involving the scores it would assign to facilities that did not voluntarily submit their quality data to Leapfrog’s survey (Leapfrog appealed that decision in September). Leapfrog’s decision not to score these has generally shifted its letter grade distribution upward, and the organization has said it is reviewing a potential methodology change for upcoming gradings to incorporate non-submitting hospitals.

Still, “a record number of hospitals are choosing to publicly report their safety and quality performance, and we applaud them for holding themselves accountable to their patients,” Leapfrog President and CEO Leah Binder said in a statement.

At the state level, Connecticut maintained its claim on the largest portion of hospitals earning an “A” grade (64.3% of its total), followed by Utah, New Jersey and South Carolina. Leapfrog also called out Rhode Island and Maine for jumping up the rankings—from eighteenth to seventh for the former, and from seventeenth to eighth for the latter. No hospitals were given an “A” grade in five states: Iowa, North Dakota, South Dakota, Vermont and Wyoming.

A hospital’s assigned grade is calculated by reviewing recent data on up to 22 patient safety measures, including a 10-part Medicare composite of reported patient safety and adverse events. Safety scores for specific hospitals can be searched on the group’s website.

Leapfrog and Binder, in a news release outlining its latest scores, made the case that its grades and similar independent measures warrant a seat at the table in a transparency conversation primarily focused on hospital costs.

“Progress on price transparency is important, but there’s no good price for bad care,” Binder said. “We are calling on the Trump Administration and Congress to ensure price transparency is integrated with patient safety and quality transparency.”

The group backed its calls by pointing to a recent analysis (PDF) conducted by the Purchaser Business Group on Health (PBGH) that reviewed employer claims, federal price transparency data, and quality and safety measures including Leapfrog’s. It “found little to no correlation between negotiated prices and standardized quality measures,” as hospitals that received high safety grades often charged cheaper prices than those in the same market with lower grades.

Leapfrog and Elizabeth Mitchell, president and CEO of PBGH, said the analysis—currently being expanded for practical usage by healthcare purchasers—is an example of how a more wholistic view of prices and care delivery should be considered when weighing a hospital.

“Employers have an appropriate duty to pay a fair price for high-quality care, and they can’t meet it by looking at price alone,” Mitchell said in the release from Leapfrog. “When we put the data together, some of the most expensive hospitals were not the safest. Our members want to buy high-quality, safe care that is fairly priced. That shouldn’t be too much to ask.”

#5719. Study raises doubts about combining vaccine, monoclonal antibody to protect against malaria

We ranked the 25 most valuable publicly traded Chinese drugmakers

Andrew covers the biopharma industry, scientific research, and public health across the continent. You can reach Andrew confidentially on Signal at drewqjoseph.71.

When it comes to preventing malaria, researchers and public health officials have been hopeful about the potential of a monoclonal antibody, one injection of which could provide recipients with several months of protection against the parasite. Such a tool, experts have thought, could give babies a layer of defense even before they start receiving doses of the malaria vaccines that have rolled out in recent years.

New research detailed Thursday has cast doubt on that strategy.

Scientists tested the monoclonal, known as L9LS, in infants in Mali, finding that it was 78% effective versus a placebo in providing protection against the malaria parasite over the six-month transmission season, similar to what has been seen in studies of the antibody in older kids and adults.

However, they also reported that it interfered with the immune response the malaria vaccine R21 elicits, resulting in a 20% to 30% drop in antibody levels generated by the immunization, according to an abstract presented at the annual meeting of the American Society of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene.

While it’s not clear what the diminished immune responses seen in blood tests would mean for the real-world protection offered by the vaccine, researchers say they’re going to focus on groups other than babies as they plan the pivotal studies that could lead to L9LS being approved, which they hope to start in 2028.

“We have these other clear use cases, so let’s get those done and get it approved and we can come back and revisit this,” said Robert Seder of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, whose lab helped develop L9LS.

There is no panacea against malaria, and various strategies come with advantages and disadvantages that public health officials have to weigh as they think about which approach to prioritize and for whom, particularly given the limited funding for a disease that predominantly affects poor countries. The infection killed about 610,000 people in 2024, the majority of them children under 5 years old in sub-Saharan Africa.

R21 and RTS,S, the two malaria vaccines, are seen as major scientific breakthroughs — they are the first vaccines against any parasite — but they require multiple doses to be effective, the first of which comes at 5 months of age. They do, however, provide some level of protection for years.

A monoclonal, on the other hand, can provide several months of protection with just one dose, which could be enough to cover recipients for peak transmission periods. (In areas with year-round transmission, deploying antibodies might require two to three doses a year, experts say.) It could offer an alternative to the current strategy of giving children existing antimalarial treatments every month during high-transmission periods, which is a cheap and effective preventive strategy but that opens the door to adherence challenges.

“A monoclonal antibody, with only one shot, provides an efficacy over six months, and those six months correspond to the season of malaria in Sahelian regions,” said Kassoum Kayentao of Mali’s University of Sciences, Techniques, and Technologies of Bamako, one of the experts involved with the new research. “In terms of logistics, in terms of programmatical use, this could be a very good tool.”

The constraint with antibodies is that they are comparatively costly, though there are efforts underway to bring down the price of each dose as researchers head to pivotal trials.

The new study enrolled infants from 1 month to 12 months, gave them either a placebo or the L9LS monoclonal, and then doses of the R21 vaccine. That sequence was what created the issue, researchers said.

The malaria vaccines work by training the immune system to recognize a protein on the parasite known as the circumsporozoite protein, or CSP. The monoclonal L9LS also binds to the CSP. That meant that, when the infants who had been given L9LS later received R21, the antibody bound to the vaccine as well, essentially interfering with the full immune response it was meant to trigger, researchers believe.

All the health and medical news you need today, in one email

Experts said there were still key groups of people who could benefit from a monoclonal and who could be the focus of future studies. Among them are pregnant people, as an infection during pregnancy can be dangerous for both parent and baby. Kids who are hospitalized with malaria are another target group. In the months after they’re released from hospital and as they recover from the infection-caused anemia, they are particularly vulnerable to severe outcomes from another malaria case. The current strategy of what’s called post-discharge malaria chemoprevention involves taking available preventive drugs every month, whereas one shot of a monoclonal as they leave the hospital could cover them for months.

André-Marie Tchouatieu of the Medicines for Malaria Venture, who was not involved in the study, said that, despite the issue seen with L9LS and the vaccine, it did not limit the potential impact the monoclonal and next-generation versions could have in reducing the burden of malaria broadly.

“Definitely there will be a use case,” said Tchouatieu, who this month co-authored a New England Journal of Medicine review outlining the advantages and challenges of different malaria strategies. “Every tool that can prove efficacy and safety will have a role to play in the whole strategy for malaria elimination.”

#5718. Animal vs. plant protein reveals a surprising testosterone divide

A new study from the University of Eastern Finland has identified an intriguing relationship between the types of protein men consume and their testosterone levels. Researchers found that men who ate more animal protein tended to have lower testosterone concentrations in their blood, while those who consumed more plant protein generally had higher levels.

The findings, published in the International Journal of Food Sciences and Nutrition, suggest that protein sources may be associated with male hormone levels in different ways. However, the researchers caution that the differences were relatively small and that the results do not establish whether protein intake directly influences testosterone.

Testosterone is an essential male sex hormone that helps maintain muscle mass, bone health, and sexual function. Although age, excess body weight, and lifestyle habits are known to influence testosterone levels, scientists have conducted relatively little research into how diet, especially protein consumption, might be associated with this hormone.

Study of More Than 2,500 Men Reveals Contrasting Protein Patterns

To investigate the relationship, researchers analyzed information from 2,546 men between the ages of 42 and 60 who lived in eastern Finland. The participants were part of the ongoing Kuopio Ischaemic Heart Disease Risk Factor Study, a research project conducted at the University of Eastern Finland.

Between 1984 and 1989, the men recorded everything they ate over four days, allowing researchers to evaluate their dietary habits and protein sources. Blood samples were also collected to measure total testosterone and sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG), a protein that helps regulate the amount of testosterone circulating in the bloodstream.

The researchers then divided the participants into four groups based on their protein consumption. A clear contrast emerged when they compared the men with the highest and lowest intakes of animal and plant protein.

Men who consumed the most animal protein had average total testosterone concentrations 1.2 nmol/l lower than those who consumed the least. Plant protein showed the opposite pattern, with men in the highest intake group having testosterone concentrations 1.1 nmol/l higher than those in the lowest group.

Similar relationships were observed for SHBG concentrations. The associations remained after the researchers accounted for age, body mass index, and several other factors related to diet, lifestyle, and health.

Dairy and Plant Proteins Show Different Testosterone Links

A closer examination of individual protein sources revealed additional differences. Higher consumption of protein from dairy products was associated with lower concentrations of both total testosterone and SHBG.

Meanwhile, men who obtained more plant protein from vegetables and sources other than cereal products tended to have higher total testosterone concentrations.

Meat protein showed a somewhat different relationship. Although greater meat protein intake was linked to lower SHBG concentrations, researchers did not find a corresponding association with total testosterone levels.

These distinctions suggest that the relationship between dietary protein and male hormones may vary depending on where the protein comes from, rather than simply how much protein a person consumes.

Despite the contrasting patterns, the researchers emphasize that the observed testosterone differences were modest. It is also unknown whether changes of this size have any meaningful consequences for health.

"Although the observed differences in testosterone concentrations were statistically significant, they were relatively small. Based on this study, it is not possible to infer whether these differences have implications for health," says Doctoral Researcher Miika Wynne-Ellis from the University of Eastern Finland.

An important limitation is that the research was cross-sectional, meaning dietary intake and hormone measurements were examined without tracking how changes in protein consumption affected testosterone over time. As a result, the findings cannot establish a cause-and-effect relationship.

Other dietary characteristics or metabolic factors could help explain the associations. The researchers also cannot determine whether eating different types of protein influences testosterone production or changes how the hormone functions in the body.

For now, the findings highlight an interesting connection between protein sources and testosterone levels, while leaving open the question of whether changing protein choices could have any direct effect on male hormone health.

#5717. Opinion: The U.S. lost measles elimination status. The next Congress should help restore it

We ranked the 25 most valuable publicly traded Chinese drugmakers

Kuppalli is an infectious diseases physician with experience in frontline outbreak response, preparedness, and policy for emerging and re-emerging infectious diseases. She writes ID Consult, a STAT column about infectious diseases.

On Tuesday, the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) announced that the United States had lost its measles elimination status, a distinction it had held for 26 years. The same lineage of the virus has spread from person to person in the United States for at least a year, meeting the criteria for measles transmission to be considered reestablished. In communities where measles is still spreading, children have more chances to be exposed, including infants too young for their first routine vaccine dose. The risk of exposure also rises for people who are immunocompromised, such as transplant recipients who take medications that suppress their immune systems.

The deaths reported this November show how quickly a decade of progress can unravel. New York reported that a child in Lewis county had died, the state’s first known measles-associated death in more than 30 years. Wisconsin reported its first measles death since 1990, an infant, and announced the death of a second child eight days later. In Pennsylvania, two deaths reported earlier in November brought the state’s tally to seven for the year. A day after PAHO announced that the United States had lost its measles elimination status, Pennsylvania confirmed its eighth measles-associated death this year, an unvaccinated resident of Clinton county.

When the current administration took office in January 2025, the United States had gone nearly a decade without a reported measles death. A month later, in February 2025, an unvaccinated child died in the West Texas outbreak.

As cases mounted last year, my colleague and I wrote in The Lancet that the Texas outbreak showed how quickly gaps in vaccination coverage could jeopardize the country’s measles elimination status. We called for sustained investment in routine immunization with targeted vaccination campaigns, strengthening public health communication and community engagement to build vaccine confidence, and resources for health departments to detect cases and contain outbreaks before they spread.

As of Nov. 13, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention had recorded more than 5,400 cases, more than twice the total for all of 2025. This number reflects confirmed cases reported to the CDC and is likely an undercount.

Pennsylvania, Wisconsin, and New York have reported a total of 11 measles-associated deaths this year. The CDC’s provisional national count is six. The agency now relies on national death certificate data, which can take time to process. State health departments can identify deaths through outbreak investigations and may use different criteria to determine whether measles contributed.

The federal death count could rise as more records come in and reviews are completed. While the CDC works with state epidemiologists on a common definition, it should explain publicly why the counts differ.

To regain elimination status, the United States must interrupt sustained transmission for at least 12 months and show, through reliable surveillance, that it has done so. That work starts in the schools and neighborhoods where children are missing doses of the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine. Two doses of the MMR vaccine are about 97% effective at preventing measles. Yet vaccination coverage among U.S. kindergartners fell from 95.2% in the 2019–20 school year to 92.4% in 2025–26, leaving an estimated 280,000 kindergarteners without the protection of both doses. Even in states with high overall coverage, measles can spread quickly in schools and communities where there are pockets of unvaccinated people.

In its first funding bills, the new Congress should protect the Vaccines for Children program and provide multiyear funding for health departments to work with schools and pediatric practices in communities with the lowest vaccination coverage. It should pay for staff who can call families whose children are overdue, answer questions about vaccine side effects, help them find immunization records, and offer appointments after school or on Saturdays. By Nov. 13, Pennsylvania’s state health center staff had administered more than 7,100 MMR doses at pop-up clinics in affected communities. Health departments should be able to do that work before an outbreak. Congress can track whether the funding is reaching those communities by asking where coverage is improving, down to the county or school district where data allow.

Some parents want to talk through their questions before making a vaccination appointment. When I helped lead Covid-19 vaccination efforts in South Carolina, and still in my practice today, I hear those questions firsthand. People want to know what the evidence shows, what we are still learning, what side effects to expect, and which recommendations have changed over time and why. They want enough information to make an empowered decision for themselves and their families.

To help them do that, health workers and public health officials need reliable access to the scientific evidence behind vaccine recommendations and time to sit down with patients and meaningfully talk through their questions.

In a nationally representative survey of U.S. adults that my colleagues and I presented at IDWeek 2026, more than half expressed confidence in the accuracy of the CDC’s vaccine information. When we asked whom they would trust if sources disagreed, 30% chose the CDC. Respondents put the most trust in their own health care providers. That trust matters because a clinician who knows a patient’s medical history can explain what the evidence means for that person and address the questions that may shape their decision.

The incoming House and Senate health committees should hold public hearings where Department of Health and Human Services leaders are asked to explain the evidence behind changes to vaccine recommendations made over the past two years. What evidence did they review? Whom did they consult? If they departed from their scientific advisers’ recommendations, why? Congress should require HHS to publish those answers when it announces a change. A pediatrician talking with a parent that afternoon should be able to explain the decision.

The same health departments that help schools close vaccination gaps also have to respond when a clinician calls about a suspected case. They need someone to answer after hours, a lab that can test a specimen promptly, and staff who can reach exposed families while there’s still time to help. Congress should fund that capacity year-round and direct HHS and the CDC to publish a plan for regaining elimination status, with clear responsibilities and deadlines.

Congress should also ask the CDC to report publicly each quarter on whether two-dose MMR coverage is rising in the communities with the largest gaps and if it is not increasing, to explain what the challenges are to vaccination. The agency should also provide information about how quickly suspect cases are investigated and where chains of transmission remain active.

These reports would help Congress understand where more help is needed and build the record the U.S. needs to demonstrate at least 12 months without sustained measles transmission.

I’ve spent much of my career responding to outbreaks after opportunities to prevent them had passed. In early 2025 when the measles outbreak emerged in Texas, I was worried that we were on the path to lose elimination status. Now I am reading reports of deaths in states that haven’t had one in decades. The next Congress should start with a hearing that puts HHS on the record about how it will regain elimination status. It should also make sure that its first funding bill allocates resources to ensure communities can vaccinate children and those at risk to stop outbreaks. Every month we wait leaves more families exposed to a deadly disease we know how to prevent.

Krutika Kuppalli, M.D., is an infectious diseases physician with experience in frontline outbreak response, preparedness, and policy for emerging and re-emerging infectious diseases. She writes STAT’s ID Consult column. The views expressed here are her own and do not necessarily reflect those of any organization she is affiliated with.
