#5622. Inside the $1.1 Million ‘Barbie Dream House’ That Started as a Goth Mansion Before Going Under Contract

A real-life Barbie dream house is turning heads in Hudson, WI, where an eye-catching pink Victorian has gone under contract after hitting the market for $1.1 million in June 2026.

With its pink walkway, bubble gum–colored staircase, and vibrant interior, this seven-bedroom, 5,189-square-foot home is anything but ordinary.

But behind its playful Barbie-inspired appearance is a spacious historical residence built in 1900 that is packed with character, original details, and incredible versatility.

“An everyday buyer interested in a classic Victorian home might think this is a bit much,” says listing agent Jennifer R. Martin of Edina Realty Inc. “It has a lot of great qualities. I would say to anyone not to let the color deter you. Painting is easy, and it’s not that expensive to make changes.”

Currently a successful short-term rental, the home is near the St. Croix River and could be used for multigenerational living or converted into a single-family home.

“The sizing alone of the house is incredible,” Martin says. “It’s enormous and goes on forever. It has two separate kitchens, so it could also be turned into a duplex.”

It is part of a collection of rose-hued homes operated by Fleetwood Rentals, which hosts everything from birthday parties to bachelorette weekends.

“The seller’s clientele is looking for a party weekend destination,” she notes. “It’s one block from the riverfront and two blocks away from downtown.”

Located 30 minutes from the Minneapolis/St. Paul airport, the property last changed hands for $614,000 in 2020. It offers “outstanding income potential,” the listing states.

“When the seller bought it, right away she had it painted in dark charcoal,” Martin says. “Her vision at that time was to have a Goth mansion that would be similar to Disney’s Haunted Mansion. It was right around the time the 'Barbie' movie was coming out, so she decided to take advantage of that.”

The multilevel home also has formal and casual dining spaces and expansive gathering areas. Original details include woodwork, built-in cabinetry, vaulted ceilings, and dual staircases.

"I envisioned the next buyer to be either another Airbnb owner or a large family who would un-pinkify it," Martin says with a laugh. "It's a great house with a lot of great qualities. I told potential buyers not to let the color deter you."

The living room has pink walls, drapes, and couches. The formal dining room has built-in cabinetry and a fireplace. The light-filled kitchen, with an enormous breakfast bar, is a surprise with its white cabinetry and a copper farmhouse sink.

The bubble gum–painted grand staircase leads to the colorful sleeping quarters. Four bedrooms are on the second level and three more are on the third floor. The primary suite has a walk-in closet, a soaking tub, a separate glass shower, and a dual-sink vanity.

Other highlights include a home theater, a hot tub, a 14-foot swim spa, and a patio designed for entertaining. The fenced lot comes with a private patio, a two-car garage, and a driveway with parking for 12 vehicles.

The property is conveniently located near boutique shopping, riverfront parks, and the marina.

"Hudson is a riverfront town with tons of history," Martin says. "People love to come here for bachelorette parties and places to go out to dinner. It also has a lot of charming, fun shops."

Kellie Speed is a contributor to Realtor.com. A Massachusetts native, Kellie attended Northeastern University for journalism, was previously the Boston editor for Haute Living, and contributed to Avalon Publishing's Moon Metro Boston guidebook. #5619. Senate Passes Controversial Permitting Bill Aimed at Speeding Construction and Lowering Costs

A bipartisan bill to streamline permitting for major infrastructure projects could have implications for both housing and energy costs.

The Senate voted 62-33 to pass the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, or BAAJA, which would streamline permits and limit the scope of government reviews under the National Environmental Policy Act and Clean Water Act. Much of that was aimed at big energy infrastructure but it also has implications for housing and even data centers.

Sens. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI), Martin Heinrich (D-NM), Shelley Moore Capito (R-WV) and Mike Lee (R-UT) introduced the bill. It's since been attached to a larger and more popular bill, but lawmakers have been debating and tweaking it for several weeks.

The latest version released this month tweaked language to assuage concerns that it would weaken environmental protections and rights of Native American groups. The bill has been popular but still divisive: While the speed would boost green energy like wind and solar power, plus electric infrastructure that lowers costs, it could also speed along fossil fuel investments, like natural gas pipelines, and nuclear power.

"Our permitting system takes too long, costs too much, and leaves too much uncertainty for the people trying to build what our country needs," Lee said on the floor before the vote, adding the bill could make "everything you buy" less expensive in the long run.

But a range of housing advocates have cheered the bill, saying it would make it easier to build affordable housing and invest in local communities. That includes the National Association of Homebuilders, YIMBY Action, the Niskanen Center, Associated Builders and Contractors, and the National Community Development Association.

"America’s housing shortage demands solutions that make it easier and more affordable to build," National Association of Realtors Chief Advocacy Officer Shannon McGahn said, adding NAR "supports streamlining permitting processes and reducing unnecessary regulatory burdens that drive up development costs, delay construction, and limit housing supply."

A White House policy paper estimates federal permitting requirements for major infrastructure take 4.2 years to complete—and produce 1,700 pages of paperwork. It expects reforms to increase the GDP by $82 billion to $164 billion, and produce $14 billion to $28 billion in tax revenue.

It also said permitting reform could cut electric bills by $178 to $251 per year for the average household. President Donald Trump urged the bill's passage in a post on Truth Social, calling it "a BIG WIN."

"This Landmark Permitting Reform Legislation will codify our America First Energy Agenda, and ensure that we can build Pipelines, Mines and Power Plants faster than ever before, lowering Energy Costs for American Families, and creating High Paying American Jobs," the president posted.

"We can lower costs, juice the clean energy economy, build big things again in America, reduce pollution, and create tons of new well-paying union jobs," Whitehouse said.

A number of groups opposed to the bill argued that some of the protections it removes would endanger protections for Native American groups and also hamstring environmental preservation.

The Association on American Indian Affairs said the bill would "threaten Native sovereignty and the protections that safeguard our country's cultural and historic heritage." The Endangered Species Coalition says it would weaken protections. Both continued to oppose the bill even as it was amended.

The House would need to vote on the bill next, and members have already began debating its merits.

"Even as amended, it undermines Tribal sovereignty, environmental laws, and locks in dangerous projects," Rep. Melanie Stansbury (D-NM) said in an X post. "This is NOT the deal, NOT the time, and NOT what the American people asked for."

Senate Majority Leader Sen. John Thune (R-SD) cast the bill as a way for Republicans to use the remaining weeks of their majority to improve affordability for Americans.

"One of the biggest things we can do to address affordability for the long term is to ensure a reliable and affordable energy supply," Thune said. “And that starts with ensuring that energy projects don’t face unnecessary permitting barriers."

The federal permitting process, he later said, "has unfortunately gone far beyond these reasonable expectations."

“And that’s due in large part to senseless delays caused by cascading litigation from environmental groups and by agencies determined to study a project to death," Thune said. “We’ve seen those delays happen to everything from water projects to broadband deployment to affordable energy and improving roads and bridges."

A poll by moderate think tank Third Way found bipartisan support for the tenets of the bill. About 62% of respondents named lowering utility bills as a top concern, and 57% keeping the power grid reliable.

“It’s more important than ever to pass permitting reform this year. The overwhelming support for the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act reflects the Senate’s commitment to addressing the nation's energy affordability challenges."

The bill was also host to Congress; latest effort to rein in data center developments proliferating throughout the country. One amendment by Sen. Ron Wyden (D-OR) would have banned data centers on public lands. Republicans blocked it.

"There is enormous concern that this bill puts the pedal to the floor on data centers across the country," Wyden said on the floor.

Following Democrat gains in the House after the 2026 midterms, a number of left-leaning groups have called for a hesitant Congress to formulate more laws involving data centers. Among them, the Chamber of Progress called for federal A.I. safety standards and requirements for data centers to cover their own costs.

A recent study by the Wharton School indicates that data centers have indeed increased industrial electricity prices in the nation. But it also said that residential customers absorbed relatively little of that price gain.

But that doesn't mean they don't impact communities. A group of Senate Democrats including Elizabeth Warren (D-MA), Chris Van Hollen (D-MD), and Richard Blumenthal (D-CT) released a report pinning other costs on them. It also critiques the tax incentives.

"This investigation finds the data center industry is bulldozing local communities and using their economic resources to play states and local communities against one another, creating a race to the bottom in which state and local policymakers feel they have no choice but to accede to the data centers’ demands — and leaving ordinary citizens stuck with the bills," they said in a joint statement.

Voter anger has put data center incentives in the spotlight. Virginia spent over $4 billion in data center incentives over 10 years, according to a state report. Ohio lost $2 billion in foregone revenue from its incentive in two years alone.

Tristan Navera is a senior reporter on housing policy, covering trends and solutions in the housing market from Washington, DC. He was previously a senior reporter at Bloomberg Law, and before that covered real estate for the Washington Business Journal. Earlier in his career, he spent a decade reporting on business and real estate in Dayton and Columbus, OH. A Cincinnati native, he holds a journalism degree from Ohio University.

#5618. The Generational Housing Divide: Millennials Had It Better Than Baby Boomers–Until the Pandemic Changed the Math

If millennials hadn’t spent so much money on avocado toast, they’d all own their dream home by now–right? Wrong. Just over half of millennials own their home. For the rest, housing costs have soared so much in recent years that skipping the avocado toast in their 20s wouldn’t have made a dent.

The story isn’t about constant struggle, though–it’s about timing. Elder millennials who bought a home in their early 30s had it better than baby boomers did at the same age: Historically low mortgage rates and higher household incomes meant those millennials spent about 27% of their income on housing at age 30, compared with 36% for boomers. Then the pandemic changed the math. Mortgage rates jumped from around 3% to nearly 7%, and home prices surged. Since rates rose above 6% in 2022, elder millennials have spent up to 35% of their income on monthly mortgage payments, compared with roughly 25% for boomers at the same age–even though millennials earn more, adjusted for inflation.

Boomers might point out that mortgage rates were much higher in their day. They’d be right: Rates peaked at over 16% in 1981 and stayed in double digits for much of the decade. But prices were lower. In the 1980s, when many boomers were in their 30s, the typical U.S. home sold for about $235,000 to $265,000 in today’s dollars. When elder millennials reached the same age–prime homebuying age–in the 2010s and 2020s, typical prices ranged from about $275,000 to $455,000.

Key takeaway: Buying at the wrong time was painful for both generations, but boomers had a better chance to recover. Falling rates throughout the late 1980s, 1990s and early 2000s gave them many opportunities to refinance into lower payments. Millennials who bought before 2022 secured historically low mortgages; those who bought later—or never managed to buy—face a much less forgiving market. Of course, it’s possible the market could become more forgiving for millennials over time; rates may eventually fall significantly enough that many millennials have the opportunity to refinance into lower payments.

This is based on an analysis of Redfin and U.S. Census data. A few notes to help contextualize the numbers: All dollar figures are adjusted for inflation. Much of the data illustrates each generation’s typical experience at a given age, combining everyone in that generation who has reached that age, whenever that happened for them. Because millennials are still aging into their 40s, for example, our 40-to-44 figures only capture the oldest millennials, who hit those ages between 2021 and 2025. All boomers have been through that age range, so their figures include the whole generation. Please see the end of this report for a detailed methodology.

In their early 30s, elder millennials who bought a home spent a smaller share of their income on housing than boomers did at the same age, despite much higher home prices. Imagine a median-earning millennial born in 1984 who bought a home at age 30. They would have spent around 27% of their income to purchase the typical home, within the “don’t spend more than 30% of your income on housing costs” rule of thumb.

Two factors helped: cheap borrowing and higher household incomes. Millennials benefited from roughly a decade of historically low mortgage rates; they fell below 3% in 2021. Millennials also tend to have higher household incomes than boomers did at the same age. At age 37, the typical elder millennial household earned an average of $100,000, compared with $88,000 when boomers were that age. The discrepancy is partly because two-income households are more common today. About 78% of women participate in the U.S. workforce, up from roughly 60% in 1980. It’s also worth noting that millennials typically work similar hours for more money than baby boomers at the same life stage.

The millennial advantage didn’t last. Mortgage rates jumped from around 3% in late 2021 to nearly 7% in late 2022, after home prices had surged about 40% nationwide during the pandemic homebuying frenzy. Rising rates often cool prices, but this time, prices didn’t fall. That mix of high prices and mortgage rates that had doubled from their pandemic-era low meant Americans had to spend a much higher share of their income to buy a home. Imagine that same millennial, born in 1984: If they bought a home at age 40 instead of 30, their housing costs shot up to about 35% of their income.

Rising prices and rates also priced many Americans completely out of the housing market, which is why elder millennials have a lower homeownership rate than baby boomers at the same age.

“For millennials who haven’t yet bought a home, affordability is a challenge. But it’s important to remember that you’re not trying to climb Mount Everest, you’re just trying to get back to 2018 or 2019, which was the last time the average homebuyer was spending just about 30% of their income on housing,” said Chen Zhao, Redfin’s head of economic research. “Before the pandemic, younger generations actually had it easier than the ones before them. But then home prices surged during the pandemic homebuying frenzy and mortgage rates shot up, while incomes kept growing at a normal pace–and the advantage flipped. If you bought in 2020 or 2021, you’re coming out ahead, but those years were the exception, not the rule. One piece of hope for younger Americans who haven’t yet bought a home: Home prices are already falling in parts of the U.S. and they’re softening in others, which means we could be headed back to 2018 or 2019 levels sooner rather than later.”

Millennials are also contending with other major expenses; childcare costs are squeezing them particularly hard. A recent Redfin analysis found that housing and childcare consume more than half of the typical American’s household income. Student loans are another big expense; millennials have significantly more student loan debt than boomers did at the same age.

Adult Gen Zers, who are in their twenties, are tracking behind millennials at the same stage of life. Gen Zers have spent anywhere from 40% of 60% of their income to buy the typical home since they’ve reached homebuying age. That’s partly because they’re still young enough that they haven’t yet hit their earnings peak, so their current income is lower than older generations, and partly because housing costs are higher than in the past. But as Gen Zers move through their careers, their earnings are likely to grow substantially, as they have for every generation before them. Combined with a gradual normalization in housing costs, homeownership should become increasingly attainable over time.

Baby boomers faced their own affordability crisis when they were young, in the 1980s. In their early 20s, the typical boomer household who bought a home would have spent more than 60% of its income on housing costs, reflecting the era’s runaway inflation and double-digit mortgage rates.

But their housing burden fell quickly as they aged, dropping to around 40% of income by their late 20s and 26% by their late 30s. Baby boomers’ homeownership rate steadily rose from about half in 1985 to over 70% by the late 1990s, and it kept climbing after that. By their 40s and 50s, the share of homebuyers’ income spent on housing had settled into the low-to-mid 20% range, lower than millennials at the same point in their life.

Much of that relief came from the same force that had hurt them initially—mortgage rates—as rates gradually declined through the 1980s and 1990s, letting many boomers refinance into far more manageable payments even as home prices kept climbing.

Millennials haven’t had the same opportunity. Those who bought before 2022 locked in historically low rates, while those who bought later faced a costly combination of high prices and climbing rates. Would-be buyers who couldn’t afford that combination were left out altogether.

“The housing market has historically been better for baby boomers than younger generations because lower home prices and higher rates are preferable to higher home prices and lower rates,” Zhao said. “You can refinance your rate into a lower housing payment, and that’s exactly what boomers did: They refinanced for up to 40 years as rates kept falling. Then home prices soared, which is why a lot of boomers are rich in real estate.”

That dynamic shows up clearly when you ask people directly. In a recent Redfin survey, more than three-quarters (76%) of baby boomers homeowners said they can easily afford their payment, while the rest struggle. Roughly half (53%) of millennial homeowners can easily afford their payment, and the other half struggle.

The same generational squeeze shows up in the reasons people are staying put in their current home. Among people unlikely to move soon, 43% of millennials cited high home prices as a reason, compared with 31% of boomers. Three in 10 (30%) millennials pointed to high mortgage rates, versus just 18% of boomers, likely because many baby boomers have paid off their mortgage and built up substantial equity. This is from a Redfin survey conducted by Ipsos in May 2026, fielded to 4,000 U.S. residents.

Consider two hypothetical couples. Alex and Jordan are millennials born in 1984 and live on two incomes, a common setup for millennial households. Pat and Chris are baby boomers born in 1956 and got by on one, more typical for their generation. The numbers below show what it would have cost each couple to buy a home to buy a home in their early 30s and their late 30s.

This analysis uses income data from 1976 to 2025 from the U.S. Census Bureau’s Current Population Survey Annual Social and Economic Supplement (CPS ASEC), accessed through IPUMS. The sample includes household heads aged 19 and older, and results are weighted using CPS household weights.

Each household is assigned to a generation based on the age of the household head in the survey year.

Home prices. We start with the 2025 median sale price of U.S. single-family homes from Redfin data ($456,409). Prices for earlier years are estimated by scaling that 2025 price back using the S&P Cotality Case-Shiller U.S. National Home Price Index from 1987 onward and the FHFA All-Transactions House Price Index for years before 1987. Both indexes are averaged by year.

Monthly housing payment. For each year, we calculate the monthly payment to buy a median-priced home. It covers principal, interest, property taxes and homeowners insurance. We assume:

Income and inflation. Household income is total household income as reported in the CPS ASEC. All income and payment figures are converted to 2025 dollars using the Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U).

Share of income spent on housing. For each generation and age, we calculate the median monthly housing payment and the median household income, and divide the payment by one-twelfth of the income.

How to read the results by age.  Much of the data in this report shows each generation’s typical experience at a given age. Because a generation spans many birth years, people born at the start of that generation turn, say, 40 in a different calendar year than people born at the end of it. For this analysis, each age point combines averages for everyone from that generation who has reached that age, in whatever year that actually was for them. For instance, millennials (born 1981 to 1996) have only had the oldest members of their generation—those born in the early-to-mid 1980s—reach their 40s so far. So when we show what the typical 40-to-44-year-old millennial paid for housing, we’re only capturing people who hit that age between 2021 and 2025. Younger millennials haven’t gotten there yet. Baby boomers (born 1946 to 1964) are fully through that age range, their 40-to-44 data point include averages from all boomers.

As a data journalist at Redfin, Dana Anderson writes about the numbers behind real estate trends. Redfin is a full-service real estate brokerage that uses modern technology to make clients smarter and faster. For more information about working with a Redfin real estate agent to buy or sell a home, visit our Why Redfin page.

Yingqi is a Senior Economist at Redfin. He studies housing market trends and explains what’s driving them for a broad audience. He previously led research on responsible AI at Freddie Mac, and also worked at Meta and the JPMorgan Chase Institute. Yingqi holds a Ph.D. in economics from Georgetown University, and his research is published in the American Economic Journal: Microeconomics and the Journal of Real Estate Finance and Economics.

Szu Yu Chen is a senior data visualization designer and developer who creates interactive graphics and data-driven experiences. Previously, she worked as a graphics reporter at The Washington Post and the Los Angeles Times.

#5617. Jon Hamm and Wife Anna Osceola Have Welcomed Their First Baby—Inside the ‘Mad Men’ Star’s Bachelor Pad Turned Family Home

Jon Hamm and Anna Osceola are officially parents! The "Your Friends & Neighbors" co-stars welcomed their first child together.

The new bundle of joy is a boy, according to a People magazine source.

The couple, who met on the set of "Mad Men," first sparked speculation that they were expecting after Osceola, 38, was seen with a baby bump during a trip to the Hamptons—with sources quickly confirming to People magazine that Hamm, 55, and his spouse were happily preparing to welcome a child.

The actor—who tied the knot to Osceola in an intimate cliffside ceremony in California in 2023—broke his silence on those rumors during an appearance on “Late Night With Seth Meyers," telling Meyers that he was "very excited and deeply terrified" about becoming a dad.

“I think I’m doing it right," he said, adding that those feelings shouldn't ever “go away.”

He then poked fun at his age, teasing, "When your kid is 70, you’ll be like, ‘I did it!’ When I’m 152.”

Back when rumors began surfacing that the couple was expecting, an unnamed insider told People, “Jon’s incredibly excited. This is something he and Anna have wanted and hoped for. He’s not thinking about his age or what anyone else has to say about it. He’s just really happy.”

The source added that Hamm is "happy, settled, and ready" for the next stage of his life, while a different insider told Us Weekly that the couple was "trying to relax a bit but are enjoying making plans for the baby."

While the process of nesting can look entirely different from one family to the next, the news about Hamm and Osceola's new addition does raise a question about whether the couple will raise the baby in the actor's longtime $4 million Los Feliz pad, which he purchased in 2017, before he was officially linked with his now-wife.

Though the home served as a bachelor pad for Hamm for several years, it has since become a marital residence for the couple and could now evolve once again—this time, into a family dwelling.

Certainly the four-bedroom, 3,600-square-foot home boasts plenty of room for a family of three. There's a spacious kitchen equipped with top-of-the-line appliances and a spacious pantry.

The 4.5 bathrooms feature spa-worthy furnishings, while the comfortable family room opens up to a stunning backyard patio complete with a built-in grill station, fire pit, and saltwater pool.

The property’s midcentury aesthetic makes it the kind of place one might picture the actor’s most notable on-screen character, Don Draper, residing, with wood paneling and asymmetrical design choices that ooze character while maintaining a peaceful environment.

The gated property is located at the end of a charming cul-de-sac in the Los Angeles neighborhood, which many big names in Hollywood have called home over the years, including Brad Pitt, Kristen Wiig, and Aubrey Plaza.

It’s not the first time Hamm has invested in the area, purchasing a 3,100-square-foot Los Feliz abode for $900,000 in 2002 with his then-partner, actress Jennifer Westfeldt. The duo parted ways in 2015 after spending 18 years together.

During his previous relationship, Hamm was not sold on the concept of fatherhood.

“I see my friends who have children and I’m like, ‘Dude, how are you even upright, much less here at work at 6 a.m.?” he candidly said to Us in 2012.

However, he’s changed his tune since beginning a life with Osceola and is now “over the moon” at the thought of enjoying a new life as a dad, according to an Us Weekly source.

“Jon has always wanted to be a dad with Anna,” the source continued. “Having a family was something that was really important to both of them from the beginning.

"They’ve talked about this chapter for a long time and were always on the same page about wanting children, so for it to be actually happening now feels incredibly special.”

The Emmy-winning performer has opened up about his desire to have a family with his wife, telling The Hollywood Reporter that, due to his parents’ divorce during his childhood, he “didn’t look at marriage as a thing,” but was hopeful for his own union to turn into a growing family.

“I will be the old dad, but so it goes,” he said in 2024, then 53 years old. “It could be a good thing. We’ll see.”

Hamm and Osceola first crossed paths in 2015, when filming the finale episode of “Mad Men” in Big Sur, CA.

Romance rumors swirled in 2017, but their relationship was not officially confirmed until 2020. The couple made their public red carpet debut at the Vanity Fair Oscars Party in 2022.

Hamm eventually popped the question. “I just knew at a certain point I wanted to be with this person,” he shared with The Hollywood Reporter in 2023. “But when I proposed, I was terrified. I was like, ‘What am I doing?’”

The couple tied the knot in July 2023, with their sentimental wedding celebration serving as a thoughtful nod to their “Mad Men” roots.

The ceremony was held at Anderson Canyon, the Big Sur spot where they first met when filming the show’s final episode. Surrounded by loved ones and lush florals, they exchanged vows alongside the Pacific Ocean.

Hannah received a bachelor’s degree in journalism from The University of Maine. In her spare time, she loves to chat about pop culture and is a major fan of reality TV.

#5616. Despite posting a solid earnings beat, Elastic sees its stock slide on rough guidance

Elastic N.V.’s stock was trending lower in late trading today after the enterprise search software firm reported earnings and revenue that beat Wall Street’s expectations but disappointed with guidance that came in below forecasts.

The company reported second-quarter earnings before certain costs such as stock compensation of 94 cents per share, easily beating the analyst consensus estimate of 81 cents. Revenue rose 17%, to $496 million, surpassing the Street’s target of $487 million.

The results helped Elastic bounce back into profitability. Its net income for the quarter came to $171 million, rebounding from a loss of $51.3 million in the same period one year ago.

However, investors were less than impressed with the company’s guidance. For the quarter in progress, Elastic said it’s looking for earnings of between 90 cents and 92 cents per share on sales of $507.5 million to $508.5 million. That’s some way below the Street’s targets of 95 cents in earnings and $517.6 million in revenue. The company is not helped by the weak Euro, with currency conversions likely to cause a $4.5 million headwind on revenue in the quarter.

The full-year picture is not much better, as Elastic forecast annual sales of between $2 billion and $2.01 billion compared with the Street’s model of $2.01 billion.

Netherlands-based Elastic is one of Europe’s most successful software companies. It’s the developer of the popular open-source enterprise search platform Elasticsearch, which is used by thousands of businesses all over the world. The base platform is free to download and use, with Elastic making money by selling a special cloud-hosted version that ships with premium features not available in the open edition. The company also sells application observability and security tools.

In the last couple of years, Elastic has tried to cash in on the artificial intelligence boom by positioning Elasticsearch as a useful cog in the wheel that feeds real-time data into large language models to provide them with business context. A key capability is Elastic Context Engine, which gathers, structures, and serves business-specific context to AI agents so they can make accurate decisions with fewer tokens and lower latency.

More recently, the company has built AI-native products including AlertZero, which enables enterprises to orchestrate teams of autonomous security agents that automate tasks around data protection and threat hunting.

Elastic Chief Executive Ash Kulkarni (pictured) said he’s excited about the potential of those new capabilities to drive significant revenue over time. “Elastic delivered another strong quarter, beating guidance across all key metrics,” he said. “Our strong results reflect expanding customer adoption and position us well to continue our strong execution in the back half of fiscal 2027.”

Unfortunately for Kulkarni, investors didn’t seem to share his enthusiasm. The market was clearly expecting trouble on the horizon in the hours before the company published its report, as its stock declined 8% during regular trading. Once the results were out, it fell another 8% after-hours. That means Elastic’s stock is now up just over 1% in the year to date.

Elastic’s stock had rallied more than 150% between April and October, but virtually all of those gains have now been erased. Prior to today, the shares had already lost more than 20% this month amid broader concerns about the AI industry. Some investors continue to worry about the potential of AI technology to challenge the business models of software companies.

#5615. This Week Brings a Chance for Clarity After Mortgage Rates Rise on Hot Inflation and Hawkish Fed Remarks

Last Week’s Highlights: No shortage of big news last week, but for mortgage rates, what mattered the most was bad inflation data coupled with a Fed that turned sharply hawkish again. Last week’s inflation data came in higher than expected and the most worrisome part was that the drivers were broad-based. It looks like core PCE, the Fed’s preferred measure of inflation, is set to come in around 0.3% month-over-month this year, or 3.2% year-over-year, which would mean that it’s moving in the wrong direction relative to the Fed’s target.

The Fed also released its meeting calendar for 2027. It will hold the usual 8 meetings, but the October 2027 meeting will be a strategy meeting where they will not change rates. As a result, they’re moving the December 2027 meeting to November. Even though this means 9 weeks instead of the usual 6 between policy meetings at the end of 2027, this should have minimal effect on monetary policy.

Finally, NAR reported existing home sales at an annualized rate of 3.75 million in October. That’s the lowest rate since August 2010 and lower than any month these last four years. This is consistent with Redfin data showing a historically low level of housing demand.

Upcoming Attractions: The biggest piece of economic data this week is the Tuesday retail sales report, which will give another look at how consumers are faring, but is unlikely to move rates much.

Investors will also get a chance to dissect the minutes from the last Fed meeting on Wednesday. And we will hear from other key FOMC members throughout the week. The ones to watch are New York Fed President Williams today, tomorrow, and Wednesday; Fed Chair Warsh today; Cleveland Fed President Hammack today, tomorrow, and Thursday; and Fed Governor Waller tomorrow.

Chen Zhao is the head of economics research, where she produces research on the housing market for public and internal audiences. Previously, she was an executive director leading housing finance and financial markets research at the JPMorgan Chase Institute. Prior to joining JPMCI, Chen was an economics consultant at Analysis Group, Inc., where she worked on financial litigation cases and led teams conducting health economics and outcomes research on behalf of pharmaceutical companies. While in graduate school, Chen was with the Center for Economic Studies and the Social Economic and Housing Statistics Division at the US Census Bureau, where she conducted applied microeconomics research using large scale restricted-access linked survey-administrative data. She started her career at the White House Council of Economic Advisers, where she focused on labor and health economics.

#5614. Mortgage Calculator: Here’s How Much You Need To Buy a $430K Home at a 7.28% Rate

Mortgage rates surged higher this week, reversing four consecutive weeks of declines as persistent inflation and geopolitical worries pushed borrowing costs back up.

The average rate on 30-year fixed home loans jumped to 7.28% for the week ending Nov. 19, up 17 basis points from 7.11% recorded the week before, according to Freddie Mac.

Borrowing costs also remain substantially above where they stood a year ago, when rates averaged 6.26% during the same period in 2025.

So what does this mean for homebuyers? Using the Realtor.com® mortgage calculator, we can look at how the math works out for the median-priced home in the U.S.

All examples assume a 30-year fixed mortgage and include principal and interest only, excluding property taxes, homeowners insurance, and mortgage insurance.

For a homebuyer eyeing the median house price of $430,000, a 20% down payment results in a loan amount of $344,000.

At today's 7.28% rate, the monthly principal and interest payment is approximately $2,354. This reflects a $40 monthly increase from the previous week’s payment of $2,314.

Compared to the 6.26% average from November 2025, which required a $2,120 monthly payment for a home at this price, today’s buyers are paying $234 more every single month.

The monthly costs have also risen markedly for those using FHA loans with a 3.5% down payment.

On a $430,000 home, an FHA borrower would finance roughly $414,950. At today’s 7.28% rate, the monthly principal and interest payment comes to approximately $2,839.

This reflects a $48 increase from last week's monthly cost of $2,791. Compared to the 6.26% rates of November 2025, where the monthly payment for this loan amount sat at $2,558, today’s FHA borrowers are paying an extra $281 in interest every month.

However, looking back at the October 2023 peak of 7.79%, where the payment for a home at this price reached $2,984, today's monthly payment still offers $145 in relief.

The long-term financial picture shows how this abrupt reversal impacts total borrowing costs over a 30-year term.

A buyer with a 20% down payment at today’s 7.28% rate will pay a total of $847,328 in principal and interest over the life of the mortgage.

While this week's jump erased much of the ground gained over the past month, this total still represents a contrast to the October 2023 peak of 7.79%, when the total cost for that same $344,000 loan would have reached $890,630.

By securing a mortgage at today’s rate instead of that peak, a homebuyer effectively avoids $43,302 in interest charges over the 30-year loan life.

FHA borrowers see a similar trajectory of long-term figures. Financing the current median-priced home at today's 7.28% rate results in a lifetime payment of $1,022,090 for principal and interest.

If that same loan had been locked in at the 7.79% peak in late 2023, the total cost would have climbed to $1,074,323. This represents a total long-term savings of $52,233 for FHA buyers.

#5613. Mortgage Mix: MBA Petitions Senators for ‘Take Care of America’s Veterans Act’ Changes; Newrez Widens Inventory

Editor’s Note: The Mortgage Mix is RISMedia’s highlight reel of need-to-know mortgage-industry happenings. Watch for it every other Friday afternoon.

The numbers: Despite mortgage rates’ downward trend for the past few weeks, the latest Freddie Mac Primary Mortgage Market Survey® reveals that the average 30-year fixed-rate mortgage increased sharply to 7.28%, up seven basis points from the previous survey’s result of 7.11%.

The 15-year fixed-rate mortgage also increased to 6.66%, up from last week’s 6.45%. Both the 30-year and 15-year rates are more than a full percentage point higher than those from the same period last year.

What does this mean: Economists generally attributed the spike in rates to inflation-related pressures, stemming from global conflicts and the rise in overall prices caused by it.

Realtor.com® Senior Economist Anthony Smith referenced the October Consumer Price Index (CPI) report as his basis for why the market expects another rate hike in the upcoming Federal Reserve December meeting.

“The October CPI report came in above expectations on both the headline and core measures, cementing market expectations for a December rate hike and giving the 10-year little room to fall,” he said.

The CPI report saw an all-items index increase of 0.4%, which is a slight decrease from September’s increase of 0.6%, but was still described as “hotter than expected,” by Navy Federal Chief Economist Heather Long.

Have an opinion on this topic? Please submit a Letter to the Editor.

Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh kept his cards close to his chest at his Nov. 16 speech and did not reveal whether a rate hike is on the table, but Fed Governor Michelle Bowman did note her disappointment at the central bank’s progress towards lowering inflation.

She stated that inflation has “proven to be more persistent than (she) had anticipated,” and pointed to the Middle East conflict, Trump Administration-imposed tariffs and “AI-related price pressures” as the main cause, in her speech to the Council on Foreign Relations.

How is the market reacting: As a byproduct of the spike in mortgage rates, the volume of mortgage applications decreased in the latest Market Composite Index from the Mortgage Bankers Association (MBA).

The MBA reported that mortgage application activity decreased 2.3% on a seasonally adjusted basis, with MBA Vice President and Deputy Chief Economist, Joel Kan emphasizing that “renewed affordability challenges from elevated mortgage rates have pushed prospective homebuyers to the sidelines.”

Overall, the third quarter of 2026 saw a significant decline in mortgage and lending activity. ATTOM reported that purchase and refinance mortgage originations were down 12% in Q3, and were down 15% compared to last year’s data.

MBA writes to Congress: On Nov. 18, the MBA sent a letter to four members of the Senate—John Thune, Jerry Moran, Charles Schumer and Richard Blumenthal—in the hopes of altering the “Take Care of America’s Veterans Act,” after its passing in the House of Representatives, and prior to the Senate’s vote on the bill.

Also known as H.R. 9237, the act is a legislative package that includes more than 60 proposals to modify compensation programs for veterans, including extending entitlements to remarried surviving spouses and establishing a supplemental monthly allowance for certain disabled veterans.

The MBA noted in its letter that they “fully support the laudable goals of this legislation” but that it cannot fully support the bill in its current form, specifically pointing out the VA Home Loan program funding fee increases.

Within the Veteran’s Act, it includes modifications to the VA Home Loan Program that would turn the Interest Rate Reduction Refinance Loan (IRRRL) from 0.50% to 1.42%, and turn loan assumption from 0.50% into 1.00%.

“The funding fee offsets in (The Take Care of America’s Veterans Act), if enacted, would have an inverse and negative impact on veteran homeowners and homebuyers (and other eligible servicemembers) who rely on their earned VA Home Loan benefit to achieve the American Dream of homeownership,” the MBA stated.

Newrez launches Personal Loans: The residential mortgage lender and servicer, Newrez, now offers Personal Loans for all eligible Newrez homeowners.

According to a release, Newrez Personal Loans are available through a partnership with Upgrade—a financial technology company that offers consumer credit products—and are issued by Upgrade’s bank partner, Cross River Bank.

“Our relationship with homeowners doesn’t begin and end with a mortgage,” Newrez CCO Leslie Gillin stated.

The release notes that the new offer expands the financial tools available to eligible Newrez homeowners, providing access to funds for a variety of financial needs. These include debt consolidation, home improvements and unexpected expenses.

Rental demand rises: Zillow’s latest Rental Market Report revealed that demand for single-family homes has risen.

Within the report, consumers noted that they would need a $14,408 pay raise to cover the monthly cost of owning a home, prior to saving for a down payment. “For a growing number of households, renting a house is a legitimate financial strategy,” said Kara Ng, senior economist at Zillow. “You get many of the lifestyle benefits, but it takes less income than owning and keeps more flexibility in the monthly budget. That’s the appeal for the deliberate renter.”

#5612. The Houses That Made New Orleans—and the Rising Cost of Keeping Them Standing

The World Monuments Fund's 2026 Irreplaceable America list recognizes the kind of architecture that has come to define the country—landmarks that serve as reminders of who we are and where we came from.

But one place was so emblematic of the country's past, present, and future that no single building could serve as a symbol of the whole.

New Orleans is the only entire city among the 10 places to receive the designation.

“New Orleans itself is irreplaceable—not just one building, one district or one monument, but the entire living city,” says Kristin Gisleson Palmer, executive director of the Preservation Resource Center of New Orleans when the title was announced.

Yet the buildings that earned the city that recognition now face a mounting threat: the cost of protecting them.

New Orleans has the second-highest homeowners insurance costs relative to property values among the nation's 100 largest metro areas, according to research from Realtor.com®. Now, as storms intensify and insurance costs rise, the city's historic homes are becoming more expensive to protect and preserve.

On a recent walking tour through Bayou St. John, Heather Veneziano—director of Tulane University's Historic Preservation Program, who helped spearhead the city's nomination—began not with a building, but with the ground beneath our feet.

The bayou that gives the neighborhood its name connects to Lake Pontchartrain, a brackish estuary fed by rivers and linked to the Gulf of Mexico. The slower-moving waters served Indigenous communities as a transportation route before European colonization.

Alongside that access, nearby natural ridges offered comparatively high ground in a landscape shaped by water, making the area an appealing, if imperfect, place to settle.

But higher ground didn't always mean dry ground. And the European settlers who followed knew the water would eventually return, and they built their homes accordingly.

“You have to build for place,” Veneziano tells Realtor.com.

At the Pitot House, a Creole colonial country house built in 1799, she pointed to the elevated living quarters as an example. The ground level, she said, could be used for storage during dry seasons, while allowing floodwater to enter below the principal rooms during wet ones.

“You lived, I think, with the knowledge that water is going to be a thing you can't fight against,” Veneziano said.

That understanding shaped the building from the ground up. Its broad roof and galleries offered shelter from the elements, while its timber framing incorporated cypress, a locally abundant wood prized for its resistance to decay and insects.

Residents adapted that approach across generations, raising homes as new neighborhoods and architectural forms developed, according to FEMA's history of building elevation in New Orleans.

But even the most carefully adapted homes can't eliminate the danger.

Today, an estimated 88.9% of residential property value in the New Orleans–Metairie metro faces severe or extreme flood risk, according to the 2025 Housing and Climate Risk Report from Realtor.com.

As New Orleans grew, new residents brought their own architectural traditions, transforming both the appearance of its neighborhoods and the ways people lived within them.

The Creole townhouse, with shops beneath upper-floor residences and courtyards tucked behind masonry facades, became a defining feature of the French Quarter.

Interestingly, its appearance was partly shaped by disaster. After fires destroyed much of the city in 1788 and 1794, Spanish authorities favored more fire-resistant construction, helping establish the brick, stucco, and ironwork associated with the neighborhood today.

New Orleans' celebrated architecture was also built on slavery.

Behind the ornate facades, enslaved people lived in courtyard quarters and worked in the homes they helped construct. Enslaved craftspeople helped construct the homes themselves, while the city's wealth was deeply tied to their forced labor.

Yet within this slaveholding society, free Black New Orleanians also established themselves as builders and property owners. Architectural historian Tara A. Dudley has documented how the Dolliole and Soulié families shaped the city's housing and built wealth through real estate, despite laws restricting Black economic independence.

Following the Louisiana Purchase in 1803, Anglo-American settlers introduced different architectural preferences. Wealthy merchants built double-gallery houses Uptown, their stacked porches and classical columns reflecting fortunes tied to shipping, cotton, and enslaved peoples.

The craftsmanship that distinguished these homes also presents a modern financial challenge.

Rami Sneineh, a licensed insurance producer and owner of Insurance Navy Brokers, says replacing handmade windows, woodwork, or plaster may require scarce materials and specialized craftspeople.

“If your home sustained significant damage, it could take months to source similar materials and you’d likely need to hire specialized craftsmen to restore those one-of-a-kind details,” he says.

An older home worth $400,000, he offers as a hypothetical example, might cost $700,000 to reconstruct with comparable details.

But not every architectural tradition emerged from wealth.

The shotgun house, which spread through working-class neighborhoods during the 19th century, arranged narrow rooms one behind another. Its origins are debated, but historians have identified possible African and Caribbean influences. Double shotguns accommodated two households beneath one roof, making efficient use of narrow lots.

And as drainage technology opened lower-lying areas to development, raised-basement houses appeared in neighborhoods such as Broadmoor and Mid-City. Their main living quarters sat a full story above the ground, carrying the tradition of elevation into the 20th century.

Yet the pumping systems that enabled the city's expansion also contributed to land subsidence, according to the Historic New Orleans Collection.

The homes remained elevated, but their protection increasingly depended on an engineered system of drainage, pumps, and levees—whose vulnerabilities became devastatingly apparent during Hurricane Katrina.

As we walked through Bayou St. John, the distant sound of a marching band practicing for upcoming Mardi Gras parades drifted across the neighborhood. Veneziano paused to listen, reflecting on the communities hidden behind and whithin the structures that surrounded us.

“The architecture is the setting for those relationships,” she said. “And people's voices are told through the built environment in which they live.”

Today, New Orleans has 26 historic districts listed on the National Register of Historic Places, covering more than 45,000 properties and roughly 40% of its urbanized area.

But preserving the appearance of those neighborhoods doesn't always preserve the communities within them.

During our walk, Veneziano pointed out double shotguns converted into single-family homes, a trend she said accelerated after Hurricane Katrina. The exteriors might remain recognizable even as two residences become one.

“It's taking away affordable housing for the rental population because there's not as many rental units anymore,” she said.

The lost rental unit also means losing a potential source of income that could help an owner maintain an aging structure.

And for the homeowners who do remain, those costs are rising on many fronts.

Single-family homes in the area carry an estimated annual homeowners insurance premium of $8,328, according to research from Realtor.com—equivalent to 3.6% of its median market value, and the second-highest burden among the 100 largest metropolitan areas.

Those estimates don't even account for the specialized demands of restoring historic architecture or purchasing separate flood coverage.

Even insured owners can face substantial out of pocket expenses. Sneineh notes that a 5% hurricane deductible on a home insured for $600,000 leaves an owner responsible for $30,000 before the insurer covers eligible damage.

“Properties that were previously affordable to purchase may now be unaffordable to insure,” says Mujahid Merchant, an independent researcher in climate risk and mortgage credit.

When private coverage becomes unavailable, homeowners may turn to Louisiana Citizens, the state's insurer of last resort, which is required to charge higher rates than qualifying private insurers.

And if a mortgaged home loses required coverage, its lender may purchase more expensive insurance and charge the owner. Merchant warns that the resulting increase in monthly payments can contribute to delinquency or foreclosure.

Yet some of the solutions draw on the same practical ingenuity that shaped these homes in the first place.

“Contrary to popular belief, you can strengthen your historic home’s roof without changing its historic look,” Sneineh says.

Louisiana's Fortify Homes Program offers eligible owners grants of up to $10,000 to strengthen roofs against hurricane winds. A state report found that median recipients saved $1,250 a year, or 22%, on insurance premiums. New Orleans also provides an expedited review process for qualifying roof replacements in local historic districts.

But even as owners find new ways to protect their homes from the elements, keeping those buildings affordable presents a different challenge.

After Hurricane Katrina, thousands of New Orleanians left for cities such as Houston and Atlanta. Not everyone returned.

Veneziano described the familiarity of living near former teachers, relatives, and neighbors whose lives have intertwined for generations—connections that can't simply be reconstructed in another place.

“You can't take what you have anywhere and put it somewhere else,” she said. “Places don't matter without people."

Allaire Conte is a senior advice writer covering real estate and personal finance trends. She previously served as deputy editor of home services at CNN Underscored Money and was a lead writer at Orchard, where she simplified complex real estate topics for everyday readers. She holds an MFA in Nonfiction Writing from Columbia University and a BFA in Writing, Literature, and Publishing from Emerson College. When she’s not writing about homeownership hurdles and housing market shifts, she’s biking around Brooklyn or baking cakes for her friends.

#5610. Google adds computer use capabilities to Gemini’s Mac app

Google LLC today released a new version of Gemini’s Mac client that can interact with other apps on the user’s computer.

The feature is available in the U.S. on launch. It requires a Google AI subscription, which equips consumer Google accounts with a broader lineup of artificial intelligence tools. The offering also includes additional storage space and certain other features.

Users can instruct Gemini to launch a local app by including the command “@Computer use” in their prompts. For example, a designer could upload a sketch of a vehicle and ask the AI assistant to turn it into a three-dimensional animation. Gemini finds the local app that is needed for the task, creates a project plan and carries out the work step by step.

The assistant supports tasks that comprise dozens of actions. Furthermore, consumers can use the output of a newly completed Gemini workflow to launch follow-up projects. A user could have the assistant generate a visual asset in a design tool and then turn it into a mini-app with Visual Studio Code.

Gemini can interact with not only local apps but also web services. That means it can load data from webpages into programs that run on the user’s machine, as well as move data in the opposite direction and between cloud services.

The AI carries out its work in a background window. As a result, users don’t have to pause their work while the assistant is running. They can track Gemini workflows via a preview pane built into the Mac client’s chat window. Additionally, Google has included controls that make it possible to give Gemini feedback mid-task.

The Mac version of Muse, Meta Platforms Inc.’s recently launched AI agent, can also interact with local apps and data. Furthermore, a cloud-based virtual machine enables it to perform tasks even when the user’s computer is offline. Dots, a competing service from OpenAI Group PBC, offers a similar capability.

Google may seek to match its rivals’ cloud-based workflow hosting features in the future. The company can also extend Gemini in other ways. Notably, it could bring Gemini’s computer use mode to additional operating systems and add features for business users. OpenAI’s Dots already includes capabilities designed to automate business workflows such as procurement.

#5609. Vitalik Buterin Wants Crypto to Have Housing’s Stability, But Can Ethereum Deliver?

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Ethereum co-founder Vitalik Buterin believes younger generations investing in stocks and digital assets instead of housing could help ease pressure on property prices. However, he says crypto still needs something that makes housing attractive: stability.

Buterin thinks that housing creates incentives for owners to keep property prices high, even when cheaper homes would benefit society. Digital assets could offer an alternative, but today’s platforms often encourage excessive speculation.

“We need the equivalent of those good properties that housing investment has, for modern digital assets,” Buterin wrote on X

His comments raise a question for Ethereum. Can the network evolve beyond speculative trading and become dependable infrastructure for people building long-term digital wealth?

One benefit of younger generations investing more in stonks and other digital things instead of housing is that it reduces perverse incentives that drive people to push to keep housing expensive, instead of rejoicing when prices drop as we do for all other life necessities.That…

Ethereum’s development roadmap increasingly focuses on making the network faster, more efficient, and harder to disrupt. Its next major upgrade, Glamsterdam, is in testing, and ethereum.org lists a mainnet launch for Q4 2026 with no date confirmed yet. The upgrade introduces several changes designed to improve Ethereum’s capacity without sacrificing decentralization.

One major feature is Enshrined Proposer-Builder Separation (ePBS). It moves the relationship between block proposers and builders directly into Ethereum’s protocol, reducing reliance on external relays and additional trust assumptions.

Another important development is Block-Level Access Lists. The feature prepares Ethereum to process unrelated transactions in parallel rather than handling everything sequentially.

These improvements could help Ethereum support more financial applications while keeping its infrastructure accessible to independent node operators. So, if digital assets are expected to become long-term financial instruments rather than vehicles for short-term speculation, this is very much needed.

Ethereum also provides an established foundation for staking, stablecoins, decentralized lending, and tokenized real-world assets. These applications could give investors more ways to hold and use digital wealth without constantly trading volatile tokens.

Yet, security, reliable applications, and responsible financial products must develop alongside network capacity.

Discover: The Crypto Presales This Q4 2026

Ethereum’s market performance presents a contrasting picture. ETH is trading just a notch above $1,800. This leaves the coin 63% below its all-time high of $4,946. The decline highlights the gap between Ethereum’s technological ambitions and its current market valuation.

Ethereum’s network utility and ETH’s investment performance are also not interchangeable. More applications and transactions can strengthen the ecosystem, but they do not create proportional demand for ETH.

The token still plays an important role as Ethereum’s native transaction currency, staking asset, and collateral across decentralized finance. For this reason, continued growth in staking, stablecoins, and tokenized assets could strengthen ETH’s underlying investment narrative.

Buterin’s comments are bigger than a debate about housing affordability. He is effectively challenging the crypto industry to build assets and platforms that encourage long-term ownership rather than constant speculation.

Ethereum has several pieces of that foundation already, including proof-of-stake security, smart contracts, and an expanding financial ecosystem.

Its upcoming upgrades aim to improve the infrastructure supporting those applications. But the network still needs to prove that its technology can deliver dependable financial products at scale.

#5608. Angelina Jolie Feels ‘At Home’ in Cambodia as She Expands Business Overseas—Inside Her Plans to Be ‘a Bit Nomadic’ After Ditching Los Angeles

Angelina Jolie is ushering in a new era after quitting Los Angeles.

In the wake of selling the $24.75 million California estate she snapped up less than a year after filing for divorce from Brad Pitt in 2017, the actress has revealed plans to enjoy more time overseas and less time tied down to a singular location.

Jolie recently visited Cambodia, where local outlets reported she met with religious leaders. The “Maleficent” star reportedly “paid her respects and presented religious offerings” to Samdech Preah Maha Sumeatheathibodi Am Limheng, supreme patriarch of the Mohanikay Buddhist Order.

She also visited a traditional craft village on Cambodia's Koh Dach, which is known as Silk Island, to observe local artisans.

The mom of six detailed her special connection to the country during earlier travels to the Philippines, where she spoke on a Nov. 11 panel alongside Cambodian filmmaker Rithy Pahn.

“I found this place and the people to be so warm and so open, and I couldn’t believe their spirits were so strong after all they have suffered,” Jolie said of Cambodia. “You go to certain places, and you just feel at home.”

According to People magazine, the actress plans to expand her creative collective, Atelier Jolie, with a residency in Cambodia in 2017.

The effort will be a partnership between Pahn’s Bophana Center and the Maddox Foundation, which Jolie founded in 2003 and named for her eldest child, Maddox Jolie, whom she adopted from Battambang, Cambodia in 2002.

According to the Atelier Jolie website, the business is focused on “the discovery of art, craft and design work from cultures around the world.” She founded the certified B Corporation business in 2023, with a headquarters in Manhattan’s NoHo neighborhood that serves as a retail store, art space, and cultural center.

Jolie spoke about her plans for the future in a September 2026 interview with L’Officiel, noting that she plans to spend more time “out of the States.”

“The hope for the Atelier was always to be global,” she said. “The idea would be to visit the different locations around the world and meet local artists and makers.”

She noted a desire to expand the Atelier to Brazil, as well as “get back to doing more hands-on work” with the Maddox Foundation in Cambodia.

She also expressed a desire to live a life that’s less tied down to one specific locale.

“I don’t really plan to have a base,” Jolie admitted. “I’d like to have a home base for my family, a place where some of the mom stuff and the family photos are. And then I’d like to be a bit nomadic for a while.”

The star also noted that she has a home in Cambodia, which “will also be a residency a few months out of the year for the Khmer culture.”

Jolie’s appreciation for the Southeast Asian country began when she first visited to film the 2001 movie, “Lara Croft: Tomb Raider.” She returned a year later to adopt her son, and has since spent lots of time traveling back and forth with her entire family.

In 2017, she directed “First They Killed My Father,” a Khmer-language biographical thriller based on a memoir of the same name by Cambodian human rights activist Luong Ung.

In a People magazine interview, Jolie revealed Maddox—who was 15 at the time—was deeply involved in the creation of the film, and helped with research.

Jole revealed her son spent “over four months” in the country at that time, “really reading, listening, learning, and absorbing all things about his culture and his country, including the very, very dark parts.”

Although Jolie was born and raised in Los Angeles, she has long expressed her desire to leave the city.

“I grew up in this town. I am here because I have to be here from a divorce,” she told The Hollywood Reporter in 2024. She explained that once her youngest children—twins Knox Leon and Vivienne Marcheline—turned 18, she’d be “able to leave.”

The milestone birthday passed this July, paving the way for a new chapter for Jolie.

“It’s the end of a certain time for me,” she told L’Officiel weeks later.

Jolie made moves quickly, putting her idyllic Los Angeles compound on the market for $29.9 million in May, seemingly in anticipation of Knox and Vivienne’s 18th.

The six-bedroom, 10-bathroom abode found a buyer in September, selling for $24.75 million. Jolie had originally purchased the home for $24.5 million in 2017, and it served as her primary residence for nearly a decade.

While Jolie plans to spend the bulk of her time jetsetting, she hasn’t said goodbye to the United States for good, and has reportedly recently purchased a Connecticut mansion, according to Page Six Hollywood.

#5607. Consumer Sentiment Jumps After Election Results

While the economy and housing still face hurdles, consumers are feeling more confident following November’s election results, according to the latest Index of Consumer Sentiment from the University of Michigan.

Consumer sentiment took a leap upward, climbing 7.3% to 51.5 in November due to “substantial post-election gains in both short- and long-run expected business conditions,” as noted by Surveys of Consumers Director Joanne Hsu. Responses were collected from Oct. 20 through Nov. 16.

“Consumers appear to anticipate potential changes to public policy under a divided government to come,” continued Hsu. “Accordingly, the expectations index surged for independents, who swung to the left in the midterms, and increased more moderately for Democrats. Expectations fell for Republicans, who may not favor a slowdown of the White House policy agenda.”

Voters have expressed expectations for the “blue wave” that swept the election to make meaningful changes when it comes to inflation and housing affordability, an undertaking that many Democrats who ran (and won) included in their campaign promises.

Sentiment is also slightly higher (1%) from one year ago, when it was at 51. Hsu noted, though, that sentiment is still “subdued” by 9% from where it was in February, prior to the start of the conflict in Iran.

The index of Current Economic Conditions also saw a monthly boost of 5.8% to 49.4, but was still down 3.3% year-over-year.

Hsu noted that some respite in gas prices during the survey period improved finances for low- and middle-wealth consumers, but “those with the largest stockholdings reported a decline in personal finances, consistent with continued AI-related agitation in stock markets.”

The forward-looking Index of Consumer Expectations saw the largest monthly leap, shooting up 8.4% to 52.9. Year-over-year, the index is up 3.7%.

Median year-ahead inflation expectations shifted downward from 4.7% last month to 3.7% this month, but remained above the 3.4% recorded in February, pre-Iranian conflict. Long-run inflation expectations also decreased slightly, from 3.5% in October to 3.3%. These expectations, however, remained above the 2.8% to 3.2% range seen back in 2024.

Hsu noted that despite consumer expectations “softening,” they “continue to report overwhelmingly that inflation—rather than unemployment—will cause greater hardship for consumers in the next one or two years.”

Claudia Larsen is a senior editor for RISMedia.

#5606. A Legacy Built on Trust and Community

Long Companies, a member of Leading Real Estate Companies of the World®

Favorite part of your job: Helping agents find opportunities and ways to navigate through them

Motto or work philosophy that you live by: Be curious. We apply our own filters and biases when we think we know the answers, so when faced with a challenge, I get really curious about why things are happening, what people need, what has changed and how we can align around that.

What is the biggest challenge currently facing your brokerage?

Rather than looking at things as challenges, I view them as opportunities—and while I believe there’s an opportunity in everything that happens, it’s about navigating that. Right now we have a market that’s starting to soften a little bit and regulate, so the question is: what do people need, and how do we deliver that?

From an industry standpoint, it feels as though a lot of brokerages and brokerage models appear to be chasing one another, but I’m more focused on quality experiences. And that begins with quality agents and staff.

I also believe the human part of this is really important in real estate. We’ve seen time and again that people want to work with a human, so doubling down on that experience is critical as we deal with a changing market.

Long Realty has reached an incredible 100-year milestone. What has contributed to the company’s success and longevity?

Having survived World Wars, recessions, depressions and pandemics, the company is adaptable and resilient. Communication is key when it comes to educating our agents so they can take that information to the consumer. We don’t make decisions blindly, and people can get behind what we’re doing, as we’ve built up a level of trust over the years.

The other thing I would point to is that we’re community focused. In addition to our own foundation that gives millions of dollars to local nonprofits, we’re also engaged in community activities, causes and sponsorships.

We’ve spent a long time building out our brand. More than just a logo, it’s the way people feel about us. A big part of my job is being a steward of the brand, ensuring that we’re doing things that align with how we want to be known.

What leadership practices have been most important in building and sustaining Long Realty’s success?

For me, it’s about empowering the people I work with. Not only do you need to work together to establish your vision, but you also need to have buy-in and ensure that people are passionate about it. And that begins with having great people who fit the culture. I find that most people want to do a great job and feel fulfilled, so how do we help our staff and our agents do amazing things? It can’t be about one person. It’s a collective, and we’re here to help the collective be better.

How do the partnerships you enjoy as a LeadingRE network member impact your business?

While we have the HomeServices network and our sister companies that we work with, layering on an organization like LeadingRE expands our capabilities and footprint. Through LeadingRE, we’ve built a lot of relationships with brokers around the country and the world, which has allowed us to service more people. We’re also members of Luxury Portfolio, which is important given the fact that Long Realty has nearly 40% market share on the million-dollar-plus side in our community. The members match our culture, and we feel comfortable referring and working with these folks.

For more information, please visit https://www.leadingre.com.

Paige Tepping is RISMedia’s senior managing editor.

#5605. Industrial monitoring startup BrightAI closes $97M investment

BrightAI Inc., a startup that helps industrial companies detect malfunctioning equipment, has raised $97 million in funding.

Smith Point Capital led the Series A round. BrightAI said in its Wednesday announcement of the deal that a number of other venture capital firms contributed as well. They were joined by GE Vernova Inc., an energy equipment company that emerged from the 2024 split-up of General Electric Co.

Many industrial machinery malfunctions affect internal components that aren’t visible to an outside observer. As a result, issues often go unnoticed until they cause a major disruption. Palo Alto, California-based BrightAI develops hardware and software tools that help customers spot issues earlier.

The first component of the company’s product portfolio is a collection of sensors called State Stickers. They’re small, rectangular devices with a ruggedized case and a long battery life. Technicians can attach them to industrial equipment to monitor for issues that can’t be detected visually.

The motion of a machine’s internal components produces noise and  vibrations that tend to follow a specific pattern. If an industrial fan’s blades rotate 30 times per minute, it might give off a whooshing sound every two seconds. BrightAI’s State Stickers can detect when a machine diverges from its usual operating pattern.

The sensors wirelessly transmit their measurements to a device called the Stateful AI Hub. It runs artificial intelligence models that analyze the data for signs of hardware failures. According to the company, its models become more accurate as the number of sensors deployed at a site grows.

BrightAI offers software that enables companies to augment the data from its sensors with drone footage. A utility, for  example, could use a BrightAI-powered drone to detect erosion at the top of an electric pole. The company’s AI models automatically draw a square around damaged components to spare technicians the hassle of manually analyzing footage.

The company says that its software can also collect maintenance data in other ways. A BrightAI-powered drone can read the meters that are attached to assets such as data center coolant tanks to check their internal pressure. Furthermore, built-in support for infrared cameras enables the software to spot overheating equipment.

The third core component of BrightAI’s product portfolio is an AI wearable. The Stateful Wearable, as it’s called, provides technicians with troubleshooting advice in the field. It also checks whether they follow safety guidelines during inspections and automatically turns maintenance data into reports.

“Our infrastructure is under more strain than it has ever been, and Physical AI has finally become reliable enough to work in the field,” said founder and Chief Executive Alex Hawkinson. “Bringing those two facts together is a once-in-a-generation opportunity.”

BrightAI says that its products monitor hundreds of thousands of industrial assets across 50,000 sites. Investor GE Vernova, which is also a customer, plans to expand its use of the company’s technology in connection with this week’s funding round. BrightAI, for its part, will use the capital to grow its international presence.

#5604. Dow and S&P 500 Plunge Into Correction as Tech Selloff Deepens

The major stock indexes extended their losses on Friday, as the Dow Jones Industrial Average and S&P 500 briefly plunged into correction territory, defined as a 10% decline from their last peak.

In midday trading, the Dow was down 288 points, or 0.59%, while the benchmark S&P was down more than 2%. The tech-heavy NASDAQ composite dropped 3.4%, wiping out all of its gains for the year.

The selloff, driven by a wipeout in tech and AI stocks, comes a day after Anthropic raised a staggering $81.34 billion during its IPO on Thursday, lifting the company's valuation to $1.414 trillion.

Anthropic shares were down 12% on Friday, giving back most of their gains after jumping 17% in their debut session.

Sevens Report Research's Tom Essaye said Thursday's selloff primarily hit the tech sector, but added that "weakness is extending this morning and, like yesterday, pulling the broad market lower (although there was no new negative news overnight in the tech sector)."

Concerns over inflation, a potential U.S. government shutdown in December, and continued conflict in the Middle East have kept some investors on edge. That, coupled with a recent spate of tech outages—the FAA outage last Friday and the Microsoft outage last Thursday—have created a sense of unease among tech investors.

AI investors were already feeling wary—as the burgeoning AI industry matures, it has yet to reach profitability. Anthropic reported $33.24 billion in revenue in the first three quarters of this year, but a $104 billion net loss for the same period.

One sector that is seemingly bucking the downward trend is real estate, which is performing better than the overall S&P 500. Real estate is up 6.95% since the beginning of the year, while the S&P is up 3.15%.

Housing stocks—especially those of major homebuilders—have shown relative strength this month due to continued institutional investment from firms like Berkshire Hathaway.

Despite headwinds for homebuilders, there are reasons for optimism following the midterm elections and the passage of the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, which passed with bipartisan support in July.

Julie Gerstein is a writer and editor based in Philadelphia. She previously worked at Business Insider as an executive editor covering news, entertainment, and digital culture, and was the company's founding Singapore bureau chief. She was also a senior editor at BuzzFeed, covering lifestyle, fashion, and beauty. She earned a B.A. in women's studies from the University of Pennsylvania and an M.A. in media and cultural studies from the University of Sussex.
